#6098. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

#6097. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

Not a Rove member yet? The program is free to join, and you can score 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link. Plus, earn an additional 5,000 bonus miles on your first hotel booking over $500 as a new user with code "BRIANKELLY500."

One of the most appealing parts of Rove for me is its loyalty-eligible hotel bookings. When you select a loyalty-eligible rate while booking through Rove, you'll usually earn 5 Rove miles per dollar spent.

But on Nov. 27 until 11:59 p.m. EST, Rove members will earn 10 Rove miles per dollar spent on new loyalty-eligible hotel bookings. To be clear, you must book on Nov. 27 before 11:59 p.m. EST, but you can stay whenever you wish.

#6094. Air India Cancels 17 Nonstop Routes: See Full List Now

Air India has made several changes to its network this year. The Indian flag carrier launched a three-weekly service between Mumbai and Toronto and plans to add Osaka Kansai to its international network next year.

However, rising fuel prices and operational constraints stemming from the closure of Pakistani airspace have forced the airline to scale back parts of its network. At the same time, it has also transferred several routes (mostly domestic or short- to medium-haul) to its low-cost subsidiary, Air India Express.

Unsurprisingly, the list includes several European routes from Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL), which Simple Flying has previously reported on. These include the Star Alliance member’s services to Birmingham Airport (BHX), which ended earlier this month, Vienna International Airport (VIE) in Austria, and Copenhagen Airport (CPH) in Denmark.

Some of the other international cuts are in the Middle East, mostly on routes to Dubai International Airport (DXB) and one to King Khalid International Airport (RUH) in Riyadh. Technically, many of these routes have not disappeared from the Air India Group's network. As shown in the table below, several are now operated by Air India Express.

Removed Austria's only connection to India

Operated by Air India Express (4x weekly from December)

Complete withdrawal from Chennai's international market

Replaced by Air India Express (5x weekly)

Replaced by Air India Express (up to 2x daily)

As for the domestic cuts, the Indian flag carrier has largely handed over these routes to its subsidiary. The Tata Group consolidated its four airlines into two in 2024, merging Vistara with Air India and AIX Connect with Air India Express. Under this structure, the Star Alliance member appears to be focusing more on its full-service operations.

Meanwhile, it has been handing over several price-sensitive, point-to-point routes to its low-cost subsidiary. Air India Express has taken over the group's operations at several non-metro airports, including Aurangabad, Bhopal, Coimbatore, Jamnagar, Jodhpur, Madurai and Tirupati. The airline now serves 48 domestic and 16 international destinations.

Yes (daily until the end of this month; restarting in April 2027)

For the current winter season, according to schedule data from aviation analytics company Cirium, the low-cost carrier has scheduled 78,202 flights, up 5.1% from the 74,374 flights it offered last winter. It has more than 70 daily international flights on its schedule and offers up to 390 daily flights across its domestic network.

Three of these are international long haul routes.

Nevertheless, we have seen some interesting additions to Air India's international network this year. In May, the airline launched five weekly flights between Delhi and Hanoi's Noi Bai International Airport (HAN) in Vietnam. The following month, it introduced four weekly flights between Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (BOM) and Tokyo Haneda International Airport (HND) using its Boeing 787-8s.

In addition, last month, it started a new winter seasonal service between Mumbai and Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ). From February 2, 2027, it will also operate four weekly flights between Delhi and Osaka's Kansai International Airport (KIX) using its Boeing 787-8s. It will become the only airline offering nonstop flights between India and Osaka.

#6093. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6092. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

#6091. Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:

The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:

Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM

The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

#6090. Just 4 Years After Launch, This Airline’s Finances Are Now “Critical”

When Norse Atlantic Airways commenced operations four years ago, in June 2022, a new dawn for transatlantic travel appeared to have arrived. The carrier promised low-cost long-haul flights using a modern fleet of Boeing 787 Dreamliners, operating from Oslo Gardermoen Airport (OSL) in Norway and, via its UK division, Gatwick Airport (LGW) in London. Now, however, the airline is on the brink.

This morning, Norse issued a statement about its financial situation and the strategic review it is undertaking as it looks to return to more stable economic ground. The carrier described its financial footing as 'critical' and underlined the need to secure financing to remain operationally viable.

Norse did not mince its words in Wednesday's statement, explaining outright that "the company’s financial situation is critical" and "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations." Given the carrier's well-documented financial struggles, Norse is exploring various options for its future.

In this regard, the airline explained on Wednesday morning that it continues to "entertain discussions for a potential takeover." Elsewhere, other options include placing greater emphasis on ACMI (wet lease) contractsto make up for its financial shortfall. The news will concern the airline's flyers and staff, and it has committed to "providing further information as and when appropriate." The airline also said it is in "discussions" with agencies to help with its finances.

"Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short-term financing. However, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution."

When Norse commenced operations back in June 2022, its first route linked Oslo with John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York City. Certain flights on this route operated via London, giving passengers flying between the UK and Norway the rare chance to fly short-haul on a 787. Norse then set up a UK subsidiary, allowing it to serve London without the Norway leg.

Today, Asian leisure destinations also play an important role in Norse's winter network. According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, Norse itself is operating scheduled flights from Oslo and Stockholm to Bangkok and Phuket in Thailand this month. Norse UK is operating flights from London Gatwick to Bangkok and Cape Town, with Orlando being its only US destination.

Fleet-wise, data from ch-aviation shows that Norse currently has a total of 12 787-9s. Of these, seven are registered in Norway, and five are registered in the UK. Interestingly, three of Norse Atlantic's five UK-registered Boeing 787s are already being used on ACMI contracts, with Pakistan International Airlines listed as their wet-lease customer.

Will Norse Atlantic be the next failed low-cost long-haul experiment?

The fact that Norse has described its financial situation as critical casts serious doubt on the long-term economic viability of its operations. Unfortunately, the low-cost long-haul market is a difficult nut to crack, as has been proven time and again over the years. Another notable example of a failure on this front involved Norwegian Air Shuttle and its 787s.

These Dreamliners operated low-cost intercontinental flights using both Boeing 787-8s (Norwegian Long Haul) and 787-9s (Norwegian Long-Haul and Norwegian Air UK). Much like Norse Atlantic, the carrier promised big things when it came to revolutionizing the long-haul scene for budget-conscious flyers. Unfortunately, the onset of the coronavirus pandemic brought these plans screeching to a sudden halt.

#6089. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6087. Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card

Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

The card also has no extra cost to add authorized users, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:

Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

Southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

Preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

On your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

That said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:

The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:

I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

If you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

If you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. #6085. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6084. I Flew A United Airlines Boeing 737 MAX From A Remote Island Airport With Just 2 Weekly Flights: Here's What It Was Like

From its regional hub in Guam, United Airlines is the only airline that provides regular air connections to some of the small Micronesian islands in the Pacific. Flying on some of these routes is a memorable experience, with local airports operating a TSA- and FAA-compliant system on sleepy little islands. Some island airports only wake up for a flight every second day. In November 2026, I flew from the island of Yap (a state in the Federated States of Micronesia or FSM) to Guam on board a United flight.

One of the most notable regional flight connections United offers is the famous Island Hopper, which flies from Guam to Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, Kwajalein, Majuro, and Honolulu, and back again. I wanted to take this flight to Majuro, but it was beyond my budget. Some United Micronesia flights operate only twice a week, meaning the flight schedule dictates the tour schedule. On the upside, many of these Micronesian flights routinely operate half-full, meaning booking out is unusual for certain routes.

Describing island hopping in Micronesia with United is often much more about the experience at the airport than with United itself. Yap International Airport is served only by United flights (with 737s) twice a week from Guam and by Pacific Missionary Aviation's (PMA) Beechcraft Super King Air 200 flights (with seven to nine passengers) once a week from Palau. PMA is set to introduce a second weekly flight next year.

As these are Yap's only regularly scheduled passenger flights, the airport is generally otherwise closed. I flew from Palau to Yap with PMA and then to Guam with United Airlines. As explained below, PMA offers the only scheduled passenger access to Yap for those who cannot pass through US immigration.

There are no direct flights connecting the State of Yap with the three other far-flung states of Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae​​​​​. To access those other islands and avoid United (and US immigration), the main alternative is Nauru Airlines. United's flight from Yap to Guam departs at 2:30 am, arriving in Guam at around 4:00 am, making it difficult to decide whether to book a hotel for the night before, the night of, or not at all. I opted not to book.

The experience of checking into United's various island flights differs significantly by island and airport. Some airports (especially on Saipan) are much larger and more sophisticated than Yap, but Yap was the one I flew through, and so I will describe that one here. Yap's check-in and baggage drop-off facilities are located in a covered area outside the building. During the check-in process, there is no air conditioning.

At the baggage drop-off (positioned before check-in), the staff informed me that their equipment was broken, so my bag would be manually searched. Many of the bags being checked in for the flight were wares in basic boxes and containers by locals to sell on other islands. Check-in was straightforward, with me presenting my current passport and my expired passport with the US visa.

One of the notable features of Yap is that the country does not collect the exit fee in the airfare. There is a window where passengers must pay the $20 exit fee before going to the adjacent immigration window. These two windows are located on the outside of the airport. After stamping the passport out of the country, there is nothing in principle to stop passengers from walking away into the night, away from the airport. Passengers wait outside the airport until the security check opens.

The carrier has launched new flights from Tokyo Narita Airport.

Even though the United flight was at most half full, perhaps a third, the entire check-in and security process was rather slow. This was particularly true of the security check. It appeared that the TSA had a representative at the station to oversee the security check, although I didn't ask, and I'm unsure. Security was one of the slowest I've seen in the world, perhaps the slowest.

Only after the security check do passengers move into the airport's only waiting room with the sole boarding gate. Located outside the airport terminal is a very basic shop selling some snacks; inside the airport terminal, there is none. The turnaround time for United flights is slow compared with main airports. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 touches down at 1:10 AM and departs at 2:35 AM.

Yap Airport lacks a Passenger Boarding Bridge (PBB) and a shuttle bus. Passengers walk from the terminal to the aircraft parked on the apron. The flight was perhaps around a third booked. I asked the local passenger next to me, and he said the flight is typically half empty. That United flight is the primary connection for Yapese, whose population is made up of around 7,000 people on the main island and 4,000 on the outer islands.

Being a modern international US airport, Guam International Airport is dramatically different from Yap. One of the most notable features of the airport is its lack of a transit area, requiring all connecting passengers to pass through US immigration. I was visiting Guam for two days, so I planned to go through immigration anyway. Due to my travel record (which includes Iran, Somalia, Pakistan, among other countries), I was questioned by CBP for three hours.

While Guam is not a particularly large airport, it is large enough to feel like a large international airport, especially after visiting remote Pacific airports. Renting cars is straightforward and easy, with my rental only requiring a $100 security deposit and not requiring a credit card. From Guam, passengers can island hop with United to Palau, the Northern Mariana Islands, the FSM, the Marshall Islands, Hawaii, and various other mainstream destinations (e.g., Japan, Taiwan).

United Airlines' Island Hopper Destinations (per United)

United is the only mainline US airline operating at Guam with a near-monopoly (99%) on local, regional, and US routes. According to the airport's report, United operated 87 weekly flights to 14 destinations over the greater region in 2024. The airport is also served by a number of Asian international carriers, including Japan Airlines, Korean Air, Jin Air, Philippine Airlines, and Air Busan. I flew out on Philippine Airlines.

The airline deploys its largest aircraft across its network, but San Francisco sees it the most.

I flew on a new United Boeing MAX 8 (registered N37319) that was delivered in 2023. The airliner is currently tasked with island-hopping routes in the region, including the Island Hopper itself. Other recent destinations include Osaka, Tokyo, and Manila. No food or refreshments are served on the Yap to Guam flight, whose flight time is around one hour and ten minutes. The lack of refreshments is perhaps welcome, as that hour was the only time I got all night to close my eyes.

While the flight is technically an international flight, in terms of aircraft allocation and configuration, United treats it as a domestic flight. The MAX 8 is configured in a two-class layout. It is fitted with 16 United First (domestic business class) seats and 150 economy class seats (including Economy Plus) for a total of 166 seats. The seats are comfortable for economy. Overall, United's economy class seems to be roughly equivalent to some higher-end, low-cost Asian carriers like AirAsia.

There is in-seat entertainment as well as in-seat charging (USB and power outlets). Perhaps due to the low capacity and the lack of competition, United's fares to Micronesian islands are typically expensive, with hops between islands often costing more than flights to destinations in Asia. As United has a monopoly in some cases, there is little choice but to accept the fares.

United Airlines dominates the international and main route connections of the island nations of Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands, along with the US territories of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. This is largely a legacy of the American administration of the former Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (TTPI) that it inherited after WWII, having conquered the islands from Japan. Eventually, the TTPI broke up and became three independent nation-states and the US Northern Mariana Commonwealth.

United is effectively the commercial successor to Air Micronesia. Air Micronesia was set up in 1968 by Continental Airlines, Aloha Airlines, and the United Micronesian Development Association. It connected the various main islands with Guam and other regional destinations. For the region, this was a major development as the islands previously lacked a viable alternative. Later on, the airline was rebranded as Continental Micronesia with Guam as its main operating hub. In time, the Trust Territory broke up, but none of the succeeding countries was large enough to sustain its own national airline providing higher-end air services.

The volume of passenger traffic is also small, leading to United flights often flying partially empty, meaning there is little scope to accommodate two competing airlines. In 2010, United Airlines merged with Continental Airlines, with the two integrating their operations. In 2017, the legacy Continental Micronesia separate operating certificate was retired, leaving the core United brand alone.

#6083. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself…

Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

Getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

Ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

#6082. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

#6081. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

If you're flying this holiday season, be sure to check your airline profile before you head to the airport.

Millions of frequent flyers are now eligible for one of the best time-savers around ... but only if they sign up ahead of time.

Over the last few months, the Transportation Security Administration rapidly expanded its new TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program to dozens of the nation’s largest airports. The new program allows travelers to quickly pass through TSA checkpoints without having to pull out their boarding pass or ID.

It's now available at more than 60 hubs nationwide, and it's a great way to speed up your trip through airport security during the year's busiest travel months.

The TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program uses facial comparison technology to help travelers breeze through the first stage of the TSA checkpoint in a matter of seconds.

Travelers passing through these lanes get their picture taken as they approach the TSA officer, and the TSA’s computers compare that image to a passport photo on file.

Typically, travelers using these fast lanes can then speed through without pulling out their wallet or boarding pass. The experience is often faster than using any other security lane, even Clear.

TPG’s Clint Henderson wrote about his experience using the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes, which are typically marked by blue-and-green signage at checkpoints.

Read more: 8 ways to get free or discounted TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear

If you’re a TSA PreCheck member or get your TSA PreCheck access through Global Entry, you’re eligible to use the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes — as long as you opt in.

To opt in, you’ll want to go to your airline frequent flyer profile, upload an image of your passport and consent to the facial identification program.

For instance, ahead of a recent United Airlines flight out of Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), I pulled up my United app. I clicked on "TSA PreCheck and travel documents."

Then, I selected “TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.”

The app prompted me to add a photo of my passport, just like you might before an international flight.

And then there were a couple of pages where I had to opt in and consent. Once you do this, you should be cleared to use the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes.

This spring, the TSA completed an aggressive rollout of the new technology to more than 60 airports nationwide.

Each of the five largest U.S. carriers now partners with the administration to allow passengers access to the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes at many of the nation's largest hubs, as well as at a bunch of medium and smaller airports.

Here’s the full rundown of airlines and airports where it’s available as of November 2026:

You’ll only be able to use the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes if your airline partners with the service at that specific airport and if you opt into the service with that specific carrier.

Also, keep in mind that there are cases (as shown above) where one airline allows Touchless ID access, while another at the same airport does not. When that discrepancy happens, it's typically because the new TSA technology is only available in certain terminals.

Take my home airport, Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU), for example. Alaska Airlines and Southwest don't offer the service here because the TSA's Touchless technology isn't available at the smaller terminal where those carriers operate. But the new fast lanes are open in Terminal 2 for passengers flying with American, Delta and United.

You should still bring your Real ID or an acceptable alternative, like a passport, to the airport even if you've opted into TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.

As I've seen numerous times at airports, technology can malfunction, or some other snafu can arise that prompts officers to ask you to present a valid ID.
