#6045. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#6044. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#6043. Rove’s Black Friday Deals Offer Up To 55% Transfer Bonuses—Plus 10x On Hotels That Earn Points And Perks

Rove is offering up to 55% more miles when you transfer to five airline and hotel programs, along with 10 miles per dollar on hotel bookings that still earn hotel points, elite night credit and status benefits. For the hotel offer there’s no stay deadline, so you can book future travel on Black Friday and collect the higher earning rate. Rove is a standalone rewards program. You earn its miles through travel bookings, shopping, dining and gift cards, then redeem them for travel or transfer them to airline and hotel programs. There’s no particular credit card you need to carry. Most of these offers last just one day. Here’s the schedule Rove gave me: November 26–30: transfer bonuses and double referral bonuses, ending at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Monday, November 30. Black Friday, November 27: the 10x Loyalty Eligible hotel offer, boosted shopping and gift card earnings, first hotel booking bonus and double qualifying miles. These end at 11:59 p.m. Eastern that night. 40%–55% Transfer Bonuses To Five Programs The same percentage bonus applies to Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Finnair Plus, Copa ConnectMiles and ALL Accor. Your Rove status determines the percentage. The four airlines normally transfer 1:1. Accor’s normal ratio is 1.5 Rove miles to 1 Accor point. Here’s what transferring 15,000 Rove miles gets you: Rove Status Bonus Airline Miles Or Avios Accor Points Member or Gold 40% 21,000 14,000 Platinum 50% 22,500 15,000 Diamond 55% 23,250 15,500 Those percentages already include the extra transfer bonus for Platinum and Diamond. Japan Airlines is worth looking at for its own flights and partner awards, including American Airlines and Alaska Airlines itineraries with three free stopovers. Rove offered everyone a 50% Japan Airlines transfer bonus in October, though. The 40% offer for most members is lower than that, while Diamond’s 55% is higher. Japan Airlines miles expire after 36 months, so a bonus doesn’t make them a good place to park miles indefinitely. Finnair is useful even if you don’t plan to fly Finnair. You can move Avios to British Airways at 1:1. Your Finnair account needs to be at least 30 days old before you can link it to another Avios program. Accor points are generally worth 2 euro cents each toward eligible hotel stays. The 15,000 Rove miles in the table therefore produce €280, €300 or €310 in hotel value, depending on status. Platinum effectively gets a 1:1 transfer to Accor during this promotion, and Diamond does slightly better. 10x Hotel Miles While Keeping Hotel Points And Benefits On November 27, new Loyalty Eligible hotel bookings earn 10 Rove miles per dollar. Rove says there are no property or rate exclusions within that category, and no promotional deadline to complete the stay. I’ve liked this feature since it launched. You can earn Rove miles while retaining hotel program points, qualifying nights and applicable elite benefits, along with the rewards from the card you use to pay. A $1,000 qualifying room subtotal earns 10,000 Rove miles. At 1.5 cents per mile, that’s $150 in additional travel value, before the hotel and credit card rewards. 5,000 Miles On A First Hotel Booking Has Different Rules Promo code BF500 adds 5,000 Rove miles to an eligible first Rove Rate hotel booking of $500 or more made on Black Friday. Join if you aren’t already a member and then take advantage of this. Rove clarified that you must never have booked a hotel through them before. Someone who’s already made a Loyalty Eligible reservation doesn’t qualify merely because this would be their first Rove Rate booking. An existing Rove account can qualify if it hasn’t booked a hotel. The code can combine with an eligible Rove elite hotel discount. However, Rove Rate bookings don’t earn hotel points or elite night credit, or guarantee hotel elite benefits. At exactly $500, the bonus adds 10 Rove miles per dollar to the booking’s standard earnings. I’ve covered a 5,000 mile first booking offer at the same spending threshold before. Double Qualifying Miles Includes Purchased Miles Boost Black Friday transactions that ordinarily earn qualifying miles will earn twice as many toward Rove status. Rove confirms that includes purchased Miles Boost and elevated earnings for elite members. For example, $1,000 in qualifying hotel spending at the promotional 10x rate generates 10,000 redeemable miles and 20,000 qualifying miles. The extra status credit doesn’t double the redeemable miles you can transfer or spend. Rove’s annual requirements remain: Gold: 50,000 qualifying miles and 5 qualifying transactions. Platinum: 125,000 qualifying miles and 10 qualifying transactions. Diamond: 250,000 qualifying miles and 20 qualifying transactions. Flat bonuses such as BF500’s 5,000 miles don’t ordinarily qualify, so they aren’t part of the doubling. Status earned for 2026 lasts through December 31, 2027. Travel counts toward the year it’s completed, while shopping and gift card purchases count by purchase date. A hotel stay ending in 2027 won’t be 2026 qualifying activity because it was booked in 2026. Higher Gift Card Earnings And The Full Shopping List Rove is offering up to 30% more miles on nearly all gift cards on Black Friday. A 30% increase would turn a 5x rate into 6.5x, for instance. (The actual rate depends on the gift card.) Rove sells gift cards marked for instant mileage earning which can help with this weekend’s transfer bonuses. You can join Rove and then you’re welcome to leave your referral link in the comments though note that this link is good for 1,500 points just for joining rather than the standard 500. #6042. Your complete guide to the ALL Accor hotel loyalty program

Answer a few questions and get your top card matches for earning maximum rewards.

Compare the cost of booking with points to cash.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

Katie Genter is a digital nomad who has traveled full time since June 2017. She writes and edits stories about points and miles, and loyalty programs, often letting her personal experiences color these stories.

ALL Accor reward points have a fixed value when you redeem them toward eligible hotel stays: 1,000 points get you 20 euros off. That gives each reward point a hotel stay value of 2 euro cents and is why TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Accor points at 2.25 cents.

ALL Accor reward points expire after 365 consecutive days without eligible point-earning activity. Any qualifying activity that credits at least one reward point extends the validity of your entire balance for another 365 days. An eligible donation of reward points can also extend the validity of your balance.

ALL Accor doesn't price hotel awards as traditional free nights. Instead, you can generally redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay. When redeeming online, you can use 1,000 points for 20 euros off or 2,000 points for 40 euros off; after that, redemption amounts generally increase in increments of 2,000 points.

You can earn ALL Accor Silver, Gold or Platinum status through either status nights or status points within a calendar year. Silver requires 10 nights or 2,000 status points, Gold requires 30 nights or 7,000 status points, and Platinum requires 60 nights or 14,000 status points. Diamond status requires 26,000 status points and can't be earned through nights alone, while Limitless status is available by invitation only.

An eligible stay paid for in part or in full with reward points can still earn status nights. However, you'll only earn reward points and status points on the eligible portion of the bill that you pay without reward points.

Accor may not have the same name recognition or footprint in the U.S. as some other major hotel groups, but its portfolio may be difficult to ignore if you travel internationally. Its brands range from luxury names such as Raffles and Fairmont to budget-friendly options such as Ibis.

The ALL Accor loyalty program works differently from many hotel programs familiar to U.S. travelers. Reward points have a fixed value in euros toward most eligible hotel stays, elite status can be earned through nights or eligible spending, and paid memberships can help you save on stays and accelerate your progress toward status.

Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming ALL Accor points, qualifying for elite status and deciding whether the program is a good fit for you.

ALL Accor is the hotel loyalty program for Accor Group. The program covers over 5,800 hotels across more than 45 brands in 110-plus countries worldwide, ranging from Fairmont and Pullman to Mercure and Ibis.

Accor has an especially strong footprint in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. Its comparatively limited North American footprint makes ALL Accor less appealing to many U.S.-based travelers.

You can become a member of ALL Accor by visiting the program's website and clicking the sign-up button in the upper-right corner. From there, it's a quick and easy process to sign up for the free-to-join ALL Accor program.

You'll see two different points balances in your ALL Accor account: reward points and status points. Reward points are what you can redeem for stays and other rewards, while status points are one of the ways you can earn ALL Accor status.

When you book an eligible stay — which generally excludes stays booked through online travel agencies — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, as well as status points based on the brand and your eligible pretax spending.

Specifically, here's how many reward points and status points you'll earn per 10 euros (about $11) spent:

So, a Classic member staying at an Adagio Access property would earn 500 reward points and 500 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending, while a Diamond elite member would earn double the reward points but the same number of status points. Meanwhile, 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending at a Fairmont would earn 2,500 status points regardless of elite tier, but a Classic member would earn 2,500 reward points while a Diamond elite member would earn 5,000 reward points.

Accor has more than 45 brands; here's an overview of the Accor Group brands:

However, not all of these brands participate fully in ALL Accor. The list of excluded hotels and brands is rather long, but note that no HotelF1 properties participate, most Ibis Budget properties are excluded and only select The Hoxton hotels participate.

ALL Accor also includes select third-party “Partner of ALL Accor” properties. Earning and elite benefits may vary at these hotels, and reward points can't be used to reduce the cost of stays at IntercityHotel, Steigenberger, Steigenberger Icon, Maxx, Jaz in the City or Zleep properties.

The ALL Accor hotel loyalty program has an entry tier, four earnable elite status tiers and an invitation-only Limitless tier. Members can also benefit from select paid memberships and occasional status match or challenge opportunities.

Status nights and status points reset at the start of each calendar year. Once you reach a new tier, you'll keep it for the rest of that calendar year and the following calendar year. To retain it beyond then, you must requalify during the next calendar year.

ALL Accor members have Classic status if they don't qualify for elite status. So, as soon as you join ALL Accor, you'll enjoy Classic benefits, including:

You can earn ALL Accor Silver status when you stay 10 nights or earn 2,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Classic members, Silver elite members get the following perks:

If you happen to have Gold status with Qatar Airways Privilege Club, you can link your account with ALL Accor and upgrade to Silver status after your first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Gold status when you stay 30 nights or earn 7,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Silver elite members, Gold elite members get the following perks:

Some cards issued outside the U.S. offer ALL Accor Gold status as a cardmember perk, though none issued in the U.S. currently do. And Qatar Airways Privilege Club Platinum members can upgrade to ALL Accor Gold status after their first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Platinum status when you stay 60 nights or earn 14,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Gold elite members, Platinum elite members get the following perks:

Once you reach 60 nights or 14,000 status points within a calendar year, you'll earn two suite night upgrades. Each suite night upgrade guarantees a one-night upgrade to a suite. You can earn an additional suite night upgrade for every additional 4,000 status points you earn.

You can earn ALL Accor Diamond status when you accrue at least 26,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Platinum elite members, Diamond elite members get the following perks:

ALL Accor also has an invitation-only Limitless status, which Accor grants at its discretion. In addition to all the Diamond benefits, Limitless members get 24-hour access to a personal assistant and concierge service, can gift Platinum status to a person of their choice and can transfer reward points to as many as five other ALL Accor members (up to 12 transfers per year).

ALL Accor offers three paid ALL Accor+ memberships: ALL Accor+ Explorer, ALL Accor+ Voyager and ALL Accor+ Ibis.

These subscriptions offer discounts, a boost toward higher elite status and various other perks. Although ALL Accor+ subscriptions can be combined, ALL Accor caps the bonus status nights you can receive from subscription programs and cobranded cards at 30 per account, per calendar year.

I've considered buying the ALL Accor+ Ibis membership, as its 15% discount could cover the 99-euro annual fee once you spend about 660 euros on eligible stays booked at the subscription rate.

You have many opportunities to earn reward points and status points with Accor. Here's an overview of the options most relevant for U.S. residents.

When you book an eligible stay — which excludes stays booked through online travel websites — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, plus status points based on the brand and the cost of your stay. Specifically, Classic members earn reward points and status points as follows:

Elite members earn additional reward points on top of what Classic members earn; Silver members get 24% additional reward points, Gold members get 48% additional reward points, Platinum members get 76% additional reward points, and Diamond and Limitless members get 100% additional reward points. However, elite members don't earn any additional status points over what Classic members earn.

So, while a Classic member would earn 1,250 reward points and 1,250 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending on an Ibis stay, a Platinum member would earn 2,200 reward points and 1,250 status points on the same stay.

You'll earn reward points and status points not just for your room but also for meals, minibar, spa and other eligible charges to your room. Plus, if you opt to Skip the Clean, you'll earn 100 reward points per day skipped. And keep in mind that you can earn reward points — but not status points or nights — on day rooms at participating Accor properties.

You can earn reward points on rental cars from three partners as follows:

You can earn reward points by clicking through the Collections site before shopping.

You can earn up to 600 reward points on your first survey with Club Opinions. And with e-Rewards, you can earn 250 reward points on your first survey.

You can convert the following transferable rewards into ALL Accor reward points as follows:

Transfers are final, though, so make sure converting your rewards to ALL Accor is the best-value option before you transfer.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

You can earn reward points as follows when you convert select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards:

After linking your ALL Accor account with an eligible airline loyalty account, you may be able to earn reward points on select flights in addition to the rewards you earn with the airline program. For example, you can earn 1 reward point per $2 spent on eligible Qatar Airways flights and 1 reward point per 2 euros spent on eligible Air France-KLM flights.

Elite members with Gold status or higher in ALL Accor or Qantas Frequent Flyer can earn 1 reward point per 4 Australian dollars (about $3) spent on eligible Qantas flights, while ALL Accor members with Silver status or higher and Azul Fidelidade members with Diamante status can earn 1 reward point for every 7.50 euros spent on eligible Azul flights.

You can earn 1 reward point and 1 status point per 2 euros spent when you host a group of at least eight attendees (or at least eight rooms) at a participating hotel. It doesn't matter whether your event is a professional gathering or personal celebration.

You have plenty of options for redeeming Accor points. As with earning, we'll focus on redemptions most relevant to U.S. residents.

ALL Accor lets you redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay at a participating hotel. You can use points toward part or, in some cases, all of your stay, although some prepaid rates require a portion to be paid by card.

To redeem points for a hotel stay online, log in to your ALL Accor account and search for a stay as normal. When you choose a rate at a specific hotel, look for one with a purple "Pay with your points" designation if you want to redeem points for part or all of your stay.

Near the end of the booking process, you can opt to redeem points toward your stay. For example, I could redeem 1,000 points for 20 euros off my stay and pay the remaining balance with a credit card.

These hotel stay redemptions provide a fixed value of 2 euro cents per point, so you generally won't get outsize value from your reward points.

You can redeem — and, in some cases, bid — Accor points for select entertainment, dining and sports experiences through the ALL Limitless Experiences page. There are some great deals to be found, too, such as this Christmas Eve dinner for just 600 points.

You can also redeem Accor points for select activities through ALL Accor Activities & Events.

It's worth checking both of these programs periodically to see whether any experiences fit your upcoming schedule and tastes.

You can redeem your Accor reward points for select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards as follows:

I don't usually recommend transferring hotel points to other travel loyalty programs, as you'll typically lose a good bit of value. Check TPG's valuations and calculate your redemption rate before transferring ALL Accor points to another program.

ALL Accor is most compelling for travelers who frequently visit Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region, where Accor has a much larger footprint than in North America. Its hotel redemptions are also easy to understand: 1,000 reward points generally get you 20 euros off an eligible stay.

However, that simplicity means you generally won't find the outsize hotel redemptions that are possible with programs that use award charts or dynamic pricing. ALL Accor also lacks a U.S.-issued cobranded credit card, and its U.S.-accessible transfer partners generally transfer at less than a 1:1 ratio.

Elite status can still be useful, especially at the Platinum and Diamond levels, which offer perks such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast in certain regions or on certain days. Finally, ALL Accor+ subscriptions may be useful for some travelers.

ALL Accor probably won't be the best primary hotel program for most U.S.-based travelers given its relatively limited North American footprint, lack of a U.S.-issued cobranded card and less-than-1:1 transfer ratios. But it may be useful if you frequently stay at Accor brands in Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region.

Reward points are easy to use at a fixed value toward eligible hotel stays, while higher elite tiers offer potentially valuable benefits such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast. Frequent Accor guests should consider whether an ALL Accor+ subscription could pay for itself through discounts, status nights and other benefits.

Even if you don't plan to pursue status, it's worth joining ALL Accor before your next eligible stay to access member rates and earn reward points.

#6040. Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.), flanked by Minority Whip Rep. Katherine Clark (D., Mass.) and Rep. Pete Aguilar (D., Calif.), leads a press conference after an incoming wave of House Democrats voted to nominate him as their leader in the next Congress, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., November 18, 2026.

We have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government. And here we are.

Fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal. He endorsed lowering the retirement age of Medicare and adding vision, hearing, and dental coverage to the program. Additionally, he said that the government should provide coverage for all children.

No doubt, with a stampede of new socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.

At this point, Jeffries’s proposal is theoretical. There’s a big budgetary difference between lowering the Medicare eligibility age from its current 65 to 60, and lowering it to 50 — as Senator Kirsten Gillibrand and other senators are proposing. There are also questions about what sort of premiums, if any, would be required for near-retirees to “buy in” to the program or how generous the theoretical vision, hearing, and dental benefits would be. Filling in those blanks is the difference between a proposal that costs a few hundred billion dollars and one that costs trillions of dollars.

But it’s preposterous at this stage to start any discussion of Medicare with a suggestion that spending on the program needs to be increased rather than reined in — especially to cover a population without a high uninsured rate. Over the next decade, the federal government is projected to spend $18.5 trillion on Medicare, making it the largest expenditure apart from that other federal entitlement, Social Security. Medicare no longer collects enough money in payroll taxes to cover current benefits, let alone added benefits that cover more people. Even a more modest lowering of the retirement age to 60 would add over 7 million beneficiaries. On its current trajectory, Medicare’s trust fund (the money it is “owed” by the rest of the government from the days when it was running surpluses) would be exhausted by 2033.

Medicare is a major driver of the nation’s broader fiscal problem. Already, debt held by the public has eclipsed 100 percent of gross domestic product. By the end of the decade, it is projected to reach 120 percent. By comparison, debt peaked at 106 percent during World War II. Now we are on track to exceed that number, not during a global crisis, but during an ordinary period of relative peace and prosperity. And that’s before Jeffries grabs the gavel with a massive majority behind him.

Perhaps more concerning, President Trump indicated last week that he may be game for some compromise proposal. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care,” he said.

If Trump is serious and actually considers cutting a deal with Democrats to expand Medicare, congressional Republicans should fight it at all costs.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

#6039. Cathay Pacific Asia Miles Announces Partner Award Devaluation, Starting January 5

Starting in January, it’ll take more Cathay Pacific miles to fly British Airways first class from Los Angeles to London than to fly Cathay first class all the way from New York to Hong Kong. The London flight goes from 135,000 to 162,000 Asia Miles each way. Hong Kong stays at 160,000. For two people booking London, that’s an extra 54,000 miles one way. A week after Chase added 1:1 transfers to Cathay Pacific, Cathay tells me its partner airlines are charging it more for award seats. It’s raising the mileage price of selected partner awards and dropping Companion Ticket Awards. The new rates kick in at midnight in Hong Kong on January 5, 2027. In the U.S., get your ticket issued before 11 a.m. Eastern on Monday, January 4 (10 a.m. Central, 8 a.m. in Los Angeles) for future travel to book at the old rates. Partner Award Prices Starting January 5 These are the nine examples Cathay shared, in Asia Miles per passenger each way. The airline says its flight award search will show prices for every route and cabin starting January 5. They aren’t revealing all the changes in advance. Miles flown · Cabin Current Jan. 5 Increase Up to 750 · Economy 10,000 12,000 20% 751–2,750, Type 2 · Economy 17,500 21,000 20% 751–2,750, Type 2 · Business 37,000 44,000 18.9% 751–2,750, Type 2 · First 60,000 66,000 10% 2,751–5,000 · First 100,000 110,000 10% 5,001–7,500 · Business 93,000 100,000 7.5% 5,001–7,500 · First 135,000 162,000 20% 7,501+ · Business 120,000 130,000 8.3% 7,501+ · First 170,000 204,000 20% Hong Kong–Tokyo falls in the short “Type 2” band. Japan Airlines business class on that route goes from 37,000 to 44,000 miles. Pick the Cathay Pacific flight and it’s still 33,000 miles for the same trip. What Happens To The British Airways Surcharge Deal? One reason to use Asia Miles has been to pay less in British Airways fuel surcharges. It’s a way to save ~ $500 each way on taxes and fees between the U.S. and Europe. However, Japan Airlines generally charges fewer miles for the same award and offers equally low surcharges. JAL is a Bilt, Rove, Citibank, and Capital One transfer partner. Flying New York–London is a distance of under 5,000 miles. Cathay gave us a new first class price for that band, but hasn’t said what happens to business class. Los Angeles–London falls in the next band up. Business class there cost 89,000 miles before last May’s increase, costs 93,000 today and goes to 100,000 in January. That 100,000-mile award will take 100,000 Chase points or 125,000 American Express points. American Express gives you 800 Asia Miles per 1,000 points. Bilt, Capital One, Wells Fargo, Rove Miles and eligible Citi ThankYou cards all offer 1:1 transfers. When An American Airlines Connection Changes The Price The biggest reason I’d transfer points to Cathay is access to first and business class seats that American AAdvantage and Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards often can’t book. Last year I flagged two first class award seats at a time between New York and Hong Kong, available only with Asia Miles. I’d still check American before transferring points. Just last week Seattle and Toronto to Hong Kong opened up in business class for 70,000 American miles each way. Cathay is keeping its Standard Award prices in place. Changes are only to partner awards. New York–Hong Kong is still 119,000 miles in business class. The oneworld Multi-Carrier Award chart which covers two oneworld airlines without Cathay, or Cathay plus at least two other oneworld airlines, isn’t changing either. Cathay says very few members used its Companion Ticket Award. If work bought you a qualifying Cathay business or first class roundtrip, you could use fewer miles to bring someone along on the same flights in the same cabin. Cathay will stop issuing companion awards in January as well. If you find the partner flights you want but might need to move the trip a day, I’d ticket before the cutoff. Changes to date only preserves the ticketed mileage price, subject to award availability and any change fee. Change the route, cabin or anything else after the cutoff and the new award prices apply. Los Angeles–London falls in the next band up. Business class there cost 89,000 miles before last May’s increase, costs 93,000 today and goes to 100,000 in January.

That 100,000-mile award will take 100,000 Chase points or 125,000 American Express points. American Express gives you 800 Asia Miles per 1,000 points. Bilt, Capital One, Wells Fargo, Rove Miles and eligible Citi ThankYou cards all offer 1:1 transfers.

The biggest reason I’d transfer points to Cathay is access to first and business class seats that American AAdvantage and Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards often can’t book. Last year I flagged two first class award seats at a time between New York and Hong Kong, available only with Asia Miles. I’d still check American before transferring points. Just last week Seattle and Toronto to Hong Kong opened up in business class for 70,000 American miles each way. Cathay is keeping its Standard Award prices in place. Changes are only to partner awards. New York–Hong Kong is still 119,000 miles in business class. The oneworld Multi-Carrier Award chart which covers two oneworld airlines without Cathay, or Cathay plus at least two other oneworld airlines, isn’t changing either. Cathay says very few members used its Companion Ticket Award. If work bought you a qualifying Cathay business or first class roundtrip, you could use fewer miles to bring someone along on the same flights in the same cabin. Cathay will stop issuing companion awards in January as well. If you find the partner flights you want but might need to move the trip a day, I’d ticket before the cutoff. Changes to date only preserves the ticketed mileage price, subject to award availability and any change fee. Change the route, cabin or anything else after the cutoff and the new award prices apply. Last year I flagged two first class award seats at a time between New York and Hong Kong, available only with Asia Miles. I’d still check American before transferring points. Just last week Seattle and Toronto to Hong Kong opened up in business class for 70,000 American miles each way.

Cathay is keeping its Standard Award prices in place. Changes are only to partner awards. New York–Hong Kong is still 119,000 miles in business class.

The oneworld Multi-Carrier Award chart which covers two oneworld airlines without Cathay, or Cathay plus at least two other oneworld airlines, isn’t changing either.

Cathay says very few members used its Companion Ticket Award. If work bought you a qualifying Cathay business or first class roundtrip, you could use fewer miles to bring someone along on the same flights in the same cabin. Cathay will stop issuing companion awards in January as well.

If you find the partner flights you want but might need to move the trip a day, I’d ticket before the cutoff. Changes to date only preserves the ticketed mileage price, subject to award availability and any change fee. Change the route, cabin or anything else after the cutoff and the new award prices apply.

I added the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card to my wallet over 10 years ago for its simple earning rates and modest $95 annual fee.

It has remained a valuable mid-tier travel rewards card due to its straightforward earning rates and no foreign transaction fees. Plus, you have multiple ways to redeem your rewards, including covering recent travel purchases at a fixed rate and transferring your miles to any of the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel partners.

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it an excellent everyday spending card. Plus, it offers 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel. These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards card an appealing and good option for consumers who want to use one card for all their purchases.

Unlike many of the other best everyday spending cards, the Venture Rewards card stands out by offering no foreign transaction fees. The card carries a $95 annual fee but offers a $50 experience credit on every Lifestyle Collection booking, complimentary Hertz Five Star status and up to a $120 statement credit (every four years) when you use your Venture card to apply for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck. Plus, cardholders enjoy price prediction and free price drop protection when booking flights through Capital One Travel.

The Capital One Venture Rewards earns miles that you can redeem for travel, cash back, gift cards, experiences and more. But you can also transfer your miles to 15-plus travel loyalty programs, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Choice Privileges.

Related: 7 reasons to get the Capital One Venture Rewards card

Related: Why I keep the Capital One Venture Rewards card in my wallet

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers cardholders several benefits that help offset the card's $95 annual fee.

One of my favorite benefits of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the price prediction and free price drop protection that's available when I book flights through Capital One Travel.

The price prediction appears anytime you search for a flight through Capital One Travel. It provides guidance on whether to book now and also estimates how pricing is likely to change if you wait to book.

If the price prediction advises booking now, Capital One Travel will automatically apply price drop protection to that purchase at no additional charge. Then, you'll receive up to $50 of the difference back if the price drops within 10 days.

These two features often give me the confidence I need to book or continue to track prices. I've gotten money back on several flights via the automated price drop protection, which is always a nice surprise.

You also have some protection if you book a flight, hotel or rental car through Capital One Travel and then find a better price for the same flight, hotel or rental car on another site within 24 hours of booking. Specifically, you can call Capital One Travel, submit a price match claim and then get a travel credit for the difference if the agent can verify the lower price.

I've successfully done price match guarantees for several flights, with the phone calls often taking under 10 minutes. Keep in mind, though, that the itinerary must be an exact match to what you booked on Capital One Travel, and you must submit your claim within 24 hours of making your reservation through Capital One Travel. The price must be in dollars and available to the general public without any coupons, promotions or member discounts.

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders receive up to a $120 statement credit for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck (every four years). The credit will apply to whichever program is applied to first, so consider your application timing if you plan to pay for applications to both programs with your card.

I love having Global Entry, as it lets me get through U.S. immigration queues quickly, and it also gives me TSA PreCheck. I'd pay the Global Entry application fee even if my Capital One Venture Rewards card didn't offer a statement credit, so this perk effectively gives me up to $120 back (every four years).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status through the "Benefits" tab of the Capital One website or mobile app. However, it may take up to 72 hours after you register for Hertz status for the upgrade to take effect, so don't wait until you're about to pick up your rental car to register.

I like having Hertz Five Star status, as it provides upgrades when available, 25% more points and a wider choice of vehicles at Ultimate Choice locations.

Each time you make an eligible Lifestyle Collection booking through Capital One Travel, you'll get a $50 experience credit to enjoy during your stay. The booking must be made in the cardholder's name, and the cardholder must be staying on the eligible booking.

If you are staying at a hotel, the hotel will apply the credit at checkout to qualifying charges up to $50. Ask the hotel which purchases qualify, then charge them to your room.

If you're staying at a vacation rental, the host will apply the credit when you book an eligible experience with a Capital One credit card. However, at some vacation rental properties, you may get the experience credit as a gift card.

You'll also enjoy other perks on eligible Lifestyle Collection stays, including complimentary Wi-Fi, early check-in and late checkout. However, early check-in and late checkout are only provided when available, and bookings may have a minimum stay requirement. At hotels, you are also eligible for a room upgrade (subject to availability).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders also get access to Capital One Dining and Capital One Entertainment.

The entertainment platform may be your ticket to cardholder-only VIP packages and hard-to-secure tickets to popular games, concerts and shows.

Meanwhile, the dining platform can help you secure hard-to-get reservations at top restaurants and provide access to exclusive dining events.

Related: Is the Capital One Venture Rewards card worth it?

Capital One miles are easy to earn and redeem yet still offer significant value. Here's what you should know about earning and redeeming Capital One miles.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers simple-to-remember earning rates. Specifically, you'll earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases.

These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards an excellent option, whether it's your only card or you use it primarily for purchases that wouldn't earn bonus rewards on other cards. I often use my Capital One Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar spent if I used another rewards credit card.

One of the big positives of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the flexibility of its miles. However, the two best ways to redeem Capital One miles are to cover recent travel purchases and to transfer miles to select airline or hotel loyalty programs.

Redeeming Capital One miles to cover recent travel purchases gives you 1 cent per mile and is incredibly easy. Once you make an eligible travel purchase with your card, you'll have 90 days to log into the Capital One app or website and redeem rewards to cover your purchase.

However, I prefer to redeem my miles by transferring them to the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel program partners. Some of my favorite options include Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Air Canada Aeroplan and Avianca LifeMiles, but you also have access to JetBlue TrueBlue, Wyndham Rewards and many other programs.

I recently redeemed 80,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points (plus $85 in taxes and fees) to fly business class from Cape Town to Perth, Australia, on an itinerary that would have otherwise cost over $2,200.

As long as you get more than 1 cent per mile when transferring miles to partners, this is the most valuable redemption option. However, TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each. So, you'll usually want to choose airline or hotel programs that offer at least this much value for your miles when you transfer them.

Related: Have the Capital One Venture Rewards Card but new to points and miles? Here’s what you need to know

The Capital One Venture Rewards won't be the right card for everyone. Here are some drawbacks to keep in mind:

If the lack of airport lounge benefits and potential difficulty in offsetting the annual fee are your primary concerns about the Capital One Venture, it may be worth considering the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card instead.

The Capital One Venture X has a higher annual fee ($395) than the Venture ($95), but it offers $300 in annual credits toward bookings made through Capital One Travel. Therefore, if you can naturally use the Venture X's full $300 annual Capital One Travel credit, it can effectively narrow the difference between the cards' annual fees to $0.

Venture X cardholders also get 10,000 bonus miles on each account anniversary, starting with the first anniversary. Between the bonus miles and the annual travel credit, most consumers will get more value than the card's annual fee each year.

Plus, the Venture X offers 10 miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel, 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases. Capital One Venture X cardholders also get access to Priority Pass lounges and Capital One lounges.

Choose the Capital One Venture X if you prioritize:

Choose the Capital One Venture Rewards if you prioritize:

Related: Capital One Venture Rewards vs. Capital One Venture X: Worth the extra $300?

A 75,000-mile bonus on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is a solid benchmark. Capital One has also advertised targeted offers of up to 100,000 miles at select airports.

As such, the current welcome offer is worth considering: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, receive a $300 credit to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year upon account opening. This offer ends soon.

This is one of the best offers we've seen for this card, and this is your last chance to take advantage of it. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth $1,688, including the credit.

Note that Capital One won't approve you for a new Capital One Venture Rewards card if you opened a Venture Rewards or Venture X card and earned a bonus in the last 48 months. So, you'll need to wait at least 48 months after earning a welcome bonus on either of these cards before you apply for the Capital One Venture Rewards.

Related: Are you eligible for the Capital One Venture Rewards’ welcome bonus?

If the Capital One Venture Rewards isn't right for you, here are a few other cards to consider:

For other options, read our story on the best starter travel credit cards.

Related: How to pick the right travel credit card for you

I've kept the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card in my wallet for more than a decade because it doesn't require much work to get value from it.

Its 2-mile-per-dollar earning rate makes it useful for purchases that don't earn bonuses on my other cards, while Capital One's transfer partners give me the option to pursue higher-value travel redemptions.

The Venture Rewards isn't the right choice if you want airport lounge access or extensive annual credits. But if you value simplicity, flexible rewards and a reasonable $95 annual fee, it remains a strong mid-tier travel card.

#6036. It Takes a Family

The answers aren’t political and institutional; they are deeply relational.

John Mulaney in Saturday Night Live’s “Sister” sketch

The recent Saturday Night Live “Sister” skit hit a nerve with its fake ad for a 24-hour elder-care service. The service is “completely free,” provided you’re the brother.

“My dad means the world to me,” it begins, with comedian John Mulaney narrating. “So, when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. I didn’t want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn’t know where to turn.”

#6035. DSA Is Right: Congressman-Elect Mocked For Refusing TSA Facial Scan—But He Brought A Passport Card, And The Photo Is Optional

The democratic socialist gets some of the explanation wrong. However, the people demanding his arrest appear to have a bigger problem with the rules than he does.

Rabb, a Pennsylvania state representative, was elected to represent Philadelphia in Congress and takes office in January.

In the video, he says he’s returning to Philadelphia from Boston. He says he doesn’t have a REAL ID card. He got a passport card so he wouldn’t need to carry his actual passport. He says TSA’s equipment wouldn’t process his identification, employees asked for another ID, and he didn’t have one with him. He also says he’d told them he didn’t consent to the photograph.

DSA Congressman Chris Rabb already working for the people by refusing to let TSA take his photo and also refusing to have an ID card. So brave. https://t.co/DnZSKeKZ7e

— Lee Kuan Yimby (@LeeKuanYimby) November 23, 2026

The State Department says a U.S. passport card can be used for domestic air travel instead of a REAL ID driver’s license. It fits in a wallet. It doesn’t work for international air travel, but Boston to Philadelphia isn’t international.

REAL ID enforcement doesn’t mean every passenger needs a state license with a star. A passport, passport card, and other documents on TSA’s accepted identification list are acceptable.

Rabb’s most useful advice is simple: Just say, “I don’t consent to being photographed.” That’s TSA’s published policy. Travelers can decline facial recognition and use the standard ID verification process instead. Rabb Wants To Avoid Being Put In A Database Rabb says he’s trying to avoid being put into another database. Too late! The standard checkpoint camera compares your face to the photograph on the ID you present. TSA says the image isn’t saved after a positive match, apart from limited testing used to evaluate the technology. You don’t necessarily have to believe them. Touchless programs can work differently. Identifying an enrolled traveler using a gallery of existing government photographs doesn’t add you to the database, you’re already there. Opting out doesn’t remove your travel records. The government already receives passenger information for Secure Flight screening. And obtaining a passport card already means you supplied a photograph. There are cameras everywhere, but for the most part there’s so much data that at least we benefit from security through obscurity. At least we did before AI made it all so much more easily searchable. I’ve covered passenger information collected for aviation security being used to help immigration agents intercept travelers. Law enforcement has access to passenger data even without this additional photo. Positive ID Matches Don’t Contribute Much To Security Positive identification is supposed to make sure you can’t simply fly under somebody else’s name. That’s necessary for the government’s database of people they want to bar from flying or ensure receiving extra screenig works. Of course, the database itself is corrupted. The terrorist screening database has over two million people in it. I’ve written about the sprawling watchlist system and agents using the no fly list to retaliate against people who wouldn’t become informants. Identity checks also serve a separate economic purpose for airlines. Matching the traveler to the name on a nontransferable ticket helps enforce price discrimination. If you could buy a cheap ticket months ahead and freely sell it to someone traveling tomorrow, you’d compete with the airline’s expensive last-minute fare. Preventing that resale helps airlines separate passengers willing to plan ahead from those willing to pay more. It doesn’t create a real aviation security benefit. I Made My Own Compromise Long Ago I’m an old line civil libertarian on this. I was late signing up for Global Entry in 2013 because I didn’t like volunteering fingerprints and a photograph to the government in exchange for easier travel. When I finally joined, before the Edward Snowden revelations, I was already writing about government collection of cellphone geolocation data, license plate readers, and other surveillance. The government already had the information, so I might as well get the benefits. At the same time, I think we’ve largely lost this argument in practice. I’ve written about the spread of checkpoint photography and biometric boarding gates becoming normal. The surveillance state has won. Rabb himself concedes that his refusal won’t make much practical difference. He sees value in reminding people they can object and in resisting normalization. I have sympathy for this. What To Do If You Want To Opt Out Bring an accepted physical ID and make the request before the camera takes your picture. “I’m opting out of the facial photograph. Please use the standard ID check.” Hand over the document and cooperate with that check. Separate a camera objection from a document problem. If the reader won’t process a passport card, ask for a supervisor and an alternative document check. Carrying a second accepted ID can save time if something fails. With millions of passengers processed per day small failure rates mean actual failures happen regularly. Escalate a refusal of the opt out calmly. TSA says you can request a supervisor or passenger support specialist. Record the airport, checkpoint, date, time, and what was said, and submit a complaint. They’ll go ahead and ignore or dismiss it. Don’t confuse any of this with arriving without allowable identification. Since February, TSA’s ConfirmID requirement costs $45. The payment covers a ten day travel period and doesn’t guarantee identity verification. Meanwhile, at the border, U.S. citizens can request an alternative inspection. Noncitizens, including permanent residents, generally cannot claim the same photo opt-out. Rabb will shortly have a better tool than an argument at a document podium: a seat in Congress. He can press for enforceable limits on retention and sharing, a meaningful manual alternative, and a way to challenge bad database entries. It won’t matter, because the security state is far more powerful than he is. But I’d be happy to see a democratic socialist spend some of his time constraining government power over travelers. Positive identification is supposed to make sure you can’t simply fly under somebody else’s name. That’s necessary for the government’s database of people they want to bar from flying or ensure receiving extra screenig works. Of course, the database itself is corrupted. The terrorist screening database has over two million people in it. I’ve written about the sprawling watchlist system and agents using the no fly list to retaliate against people who wouldn’t become informants. Identity checks also serve a separate economic purpose for airlines. Matching the traveler to the name on a nontransferable ticket helps enforce price discrimination. If you could buy a cheap ticket months ahead and freely sell it to someone traveling tomorrow, you’d compete with the airline’s expensive last-minute fare. Preventing that resale helps airlines separate passengers willing to plan ahead from those willing to pay more. It doesn’t create a real aviation security benefit. I Made My Own Compromise Long Ago I’m an old line civil libertarian on this. I was late signing up for Global Entry in 2013 because I didn’t like volunteering fingerprints and a photograph to the government in exchange for easier travel. When I finally joined, before the Edward Snowden revelations, I was already writing about government collection of cellphone geolocation data, license plate readers, and other surveillance. The government already had the information, so I might as well get the benefits. At the same time, I think we’ve largely lost this argument in practice. I’ve written about the spread of checkpoint photography and biometric boarding gates becoming normal. The surveillance state has won. Rabb himself concedes that his refusal won’t make much practical difference. He sees value in reminding people they can object and in resisting normalization. I have sympathy for this. What To Do If You Want To Opt Out Bring an accepted physical ID and make the request before the camera takes your picture. “I’m opting out of the facial photograph. Please use the standard ID check.” Hand over the document and cooperate with that check. Separate a camera objection from a document problem. If the reader won’t process a passport card, ask for a supervisor and an alternative document check. Carrying a second accepted ID can save time if something fails. With millions of passengers processed per day small failure rates mean actual failures happen regularly. Escalate a refusal of the opt out calmly. TSA says you can request a supervisor or passenger support specialist. Record the airport, checkpoint, date, time, and what was said, and submit a complaint. They’ll go ahead and ignore or dismiss it. Don’t confuse any of this with arriving without allowable identification. Since February, TSA’s ConfirmID requirement costs $45. The payment covers a ten day travel period and doesn’t guarantee identity verification. Meanwhile, at the border, U.S. citizens can request an alternative inspection. Noncitizens, including permanent residents, generally cannot claim the same photo opt-out. Rabb will shortly have a better tool than an argument at a document podium: a seat in Congress. He can press for enforceable limits on retention and sharing, a meaningful manual alternative, and a way to challenge bad database entries. It won’t matter, because the security state is far more powerful than he is. But I’d be happy to see a democratic socialist spend some of his time constraining government power over travelers. Separate a camera objection from a document problem. If the reader won’t process a passport card, ask for a supervisor and an alternative document check. Carrying a second accepted ID can save time if something fails. With millions of passengers processed per day small failure rates mean actual failures happen regularly.

Escalate a refusal of the opt out calmly. TSA says you can request a supervisor or passenger support specialist. Record the airport, checkpoint, date, time, and what was said, and submit a complaint. They’ll go ahead and ignore or dismiss it.

Rabb will shortly have a better tool than an argument at a document podium: a seat in Congress. #6034. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6033. Thieves Are Stealing Used Cooking Oil From Hotels—It May Be Fueling Your Next Flight

Thieves stole 350 gallons of cooking oil from an airport hotel in Pennsylvania. The haul was valued at $2,100, and the victim named by state police was a biofuel company. Hotel kitchen grease has become valuable enough to steal. Used grease can fetch more than new! And it can eventually wind up fueling an airline flight and helping a carrier meet its environmental goals. Pennsylvania State Police responded on November 18 to the theft at 3400 Airport Road, the Days Hotel by Wyndham Allentown Airport / Lehigh Valley. The hotel has a restaurant and banquet facilities, so there’s a kitchen generating oil to collect. The loss works out to $6 per gallon. The listed victim was Buffalo Biodiesel, which deals in used cooking oil, which it processes and sends to biodiesel refineries. People steal astonishing things from hotels. I’ve covered mattresses, a lobby grand piano, and even a fireplace being taken. Two men carried an entire ATM out of a Country Inn & Suites. Used fryer oil seems much less attractive? But there’s a ready buyer for it, and hotels have been caught up in a much broader rash of cooking oil thefts: Hilton Short Hills, New Jersey: Police caught two men taking cooking oil around 3 a.m.. They’d arrived in a white Penske truck and were charged with theft and conspiracy. Brick Hotel, Pennsylvania: An attempted theft caused a used oil spill that required an environmental cleanup and closed a municipal parking lot. A hotel in Largs, Scotland: Two men arrived in a van around 1 a.m. and carried away cooking oil in blue buckets in order to convert it into biodiesel for profit. Old Ground Hotel, Ireland: Two men who pleaded guilty to stealing used cooking oil said they wanted it to fuel their cars. In September, two defendants pleaded guilty in a federal case involving 19 people charged over a cooking oil theft operation spanning ten states. Trucks were taking the oil from restaurant collection tanks, warehouses consolidated it, the oil was sold across states and the effort was implicated in money laundering. The North American Renderers Association estimates annual used cooking oil theft at $300 million to $500 million. Once a hotel is done frying food, the oil can be collected and sold for processing into fuel. Buffalo Biodiesel supplies collection containers, picks up the oil, and processes it at its Tonawanda, New York facility before shipping it to refineries. These are the company’s processing tanks: Used cooking oil gets processed into sustainable aviation fuel. Refineries turn the fats and oils into fuel that can be blended with conventional jet fuel. Airlines want that fuel to meet environmental targets, and government subsidies prop up that market. This can create some very strange incentives. I’ve written about the arbitrage that makes used cooking oil more valuable than new oil in Malaysia. The government subsidizes cooking oil for food. Meanwhile, the biofuel market pays for oil classified as waste. In July 2025, subsidized fresh oil sold for 2.50 ringgit per kilogram while collectors could pay up to 3.50 ringgit for used oil. That’s a 40% spread. This turns into a greenwashing scam that actually creates more problems than it solves. By paying for “used” oil restaurants are encouraged to ‘create’ used oil, replacing their oil sooner. When you pay more than fresh oil costs, the incentive actually becomes skipping the cooking part altogether. But the environmental case depends on making use of waste that already exists. Instead, diverting fresh palm oil into that market increases the demand for new cooling oil production (and the pressure to clear land for it). The Simpsons got to this in 1998. In “Lard of the Dance,” Homer discovers that used grease has resale value: “Used grease is worth money? Then my arteries are clogged with yellow gold!” He and Bart eventually try stealing the school’s grease. Groundskeeper Willie catches them — he’s been saving it for retirement. Once a hotel is done frying food, the oil can be collected and sold for processing into fuel. Buffalo Biodiesel supplies collection containers, picks up the oil, and processes it at its Tonawanda, New York facility before shipping it to refineries. These are the company’s processing tanks:

#6032. Fiscal Reality Interrupts Everyone’s Social Security Fairy Tales

It turns out that we were right all along.

Senator Bill Cassidy (R., La.), left, President Donald Trump, right.

The most important revelation in the news that President Trump is working with his outgoing senatorial rival, Bill Cassidy, on a package of Social Security reforms is obvious: The math comes for us all, without fear or favor, and trade-offs are unavoidable even if voters hate hearing about them.

But there’s another important element to today’s news that should not go unacknowledged: We were right.
