Is Norwegian Luna the best big new ship sailing out of Miami?

For someone looking for a vessel that feels more refined and upscale than what is typical among big Miami-based ships, it just might be. (Its sister ship, Norwegian Aqua, also sails from Miami.)

As I saw during a week on board in October, Norwegian Luna has an elevated design compared to many of the big new ships sailing out of Miami, giving it an elegance that stands out among the competition.

That said, for someone who just wants the widest array of onboard amusements, entertainment and nightlife that they can find on a cruise ship, the choice gets harder.

Although its large, the eight-month-old Norwegian Luna — the latest in Norwegian Cruise Line's Prima Plus class — is notably smaller than the other big new ships that it is up against in Miami. That means there's less room for the wide range of attractions you'll find on those vessels.

Unlike two of its biggest rivals in the market, Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas and MSC Cruises' MSC World America, for instance, it lacks a water park area with multiple waterslides on its top deck (though it does have one large water attraction, the Aqua Slidecoaster). It also has fewer and smaller main pool areas. That's a real strike against it for families with kids, in particular.

As someone who generally prefers more intimate and elegant ships, I know which side of the trade-off I'm on. If it were my money, I'd lean toward Norwegian Luna. It's the perfect big ship for me.

But read on to see if it's right for you.

Unveiled in March, Norwegian Luna is the second ship in Norwegian's new Prima Plus Class of vessels, following the year-old Norwegian Aqua.

These two ships, along with two similar but slightly smaller Prima Class vessels that debuted in 2022 and 2023, are smaller than the ships that Norwegian launched just before them, which is a bit unusual. Most of Norwegian's competitors, such as Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises, have been rolling out ever bigger ships, loaded with ever more onboard attractions and venues.

Related: Norwegian Cruise Line ships ranked from biggest to smallest

For now, Norwegian Luna mostly operates seven-night voyages to the Caribbean out of Miami on Saturdays, competing head-to-head with new ships from Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises (Icon of the Seas and MSC World America) that are much bigger.

Those two ships, notably, are 59% and 38% bigger than Luna, respectively, allowing for a lot more onboard venues of all kinds, from decktop attractions to showrooms, restaurants and bars.

On the flip side, Norwegian Luna's smaller size, coupled with its elevated design, generally contributes to a more intimate and elegant feel — a significant differentiator.

I say "generally," as Norwegian Luna's more elegant feel is sometimes punctured by aggressive upselling and extra charges that are incongruous with the ship's overall vibe.

It's not a dealbreaker, but it's off-putting at times and something you need to be prepared for going into a sailing.

Cabins are a strong point on Norwegian Luna. The majority of balcony cabins (the biggest category of cabins on the ship) are surprisingly spacious at 358 square feet, with a clean-lined, modern design and solid storage. I particularly love the bathrooms, which offer larger showers than you sometimes get on mass-market ships as well as a clever pivot door that makes them easy to enter.

Balcony cabins account for about 57% of Norwegian Luna's 1,813 cabins. But there are also 140 oceanview cabins without balconies of various sizes and 424 windowless "inside" cabins that offer a modern design with solid storage.

The latter category includes 73 very small but perfect-for-one solo cabins, known as Studios, in a keycard-access-only solo area with its own lounge — a Norwegian signature. Norwegian has leaned into the solo cruise market in recent years with these exclusive solo areas, and the cabins are in high demand. Book one early if you want one.

Norwegian Luna is also home to one of the line's signature The Haven suite complexes. These are separate, keycard-access-only enclaves found on many Norwegian ships that not only have a wide range of lovely suites but also their own private restaurants, lounges and bars, and outdoor sun and pool decks.

On Norwegian Luna, this complex (tied with the one on Norwegian Aqua as the biggest in the fleet) fills the top four decks of the back of the ship, accessible via its own private elevator. It's truly wonderful. Staying in one of its suites — there are 123, including 25 Owner's Suites that measure up to an astounding 2,100 square feet — feels like staying in a completely different, far more upscale vessel.

Among my favorite features of Norwegian Luna's Haven area is its cozy bar, which offers a much-upgraded bar experience to what you'll find anywhere else on the ship. There are higher-end spirits and creative craft cocktails made by some of the best bartenders at sea.

In addition to the suites in The Haven, you'll find additional suites and penthouses outside the area that also come with extra privileges but not all the perks that Haven guests receive.

Pro tip: If you are sensitive to noise, steer clear of cabins with connecting doors to adjacent cabins (you'll find them noted on Norwegian Luna's deck plans). Even when closed, their imperfect seals will cause you to hear noise from the cabin next door.

Norwegian ships have always been known for a wide range of restaurant choices, and Norwegian Luna is no exception. It has more than a dozen sit-down eateries, ranging from a super-casual food hall to a high-end steakhouse — some quite good for a big, mass-market ship.

Just be warned that the restaurant scene on Norwegian Luna is one of the areas where you'll encounter a lot of upcharges, with both high cover charges for some restaurants and additional charges for individual menu items that can really push up the bill.

Among the priciest eateries on board are Norwegian's two signature restaurants, Cagney's Steakhouse (found on every Norwegian ship) and the French-focused Le Bistro (found on nearly every Norwegian ship). Both have cover charges of $60 per person that rise to $72 per person with a mandatory 20% gratuity; that price can climb even higher if you order an item with an upcharge.

Both are elegant and upscale, and serve quality dishes, as does Palomar, which serves seafood-focused Mediterranean cuisine for the same $60 cover charge. I highly recommend Palomar's whole fish-for-two baked in salt, which is well worth its additional $25 charge ($30 with the mandatory gratuity) — not just because it's a showy dish that tastes as good as it looks, but because it's deboned tableside, adding some tableside theatrics to the evening.

Other extra-charge eateries include Los Lobos ($40 per person), which dishes out Mexican cuisine; Nama Sushi & Sashimi ($50 per person), for its namesake Japanese cuisine; Japanese hibachi restaurant Hasuki ($60 per person); and Thai-centered Sukothai ($50 per person).

All of these have mandatory 20% gratuity charges on top of their cover charges, as does Onda by Scarpetta, which is an Italian eatery ($40 per person) with ties to New York City's high-end Scarpetta restaurant. The latter is one eatery I'd skip, as the cuisine is spotty and the service more rushed than relaxing. (Despite ordering four courses, we were barely there an hour as the dishes were raced out to us one on top of the other.)

For those keeping to a tight budget, there are fortunately plenty of solid included-in-the-fare options on Norwegian Luna, too.

The real standout here is Indulge Food Hall, a casual, multi-outlet venue with separate stands and counters serving tapas, Indian dishes, noodles, vegetarian bowls, barbecue, Latin and Mexican food, and rotisserie items. Some of these items, particularly the Indian dishes (which include chicken tikka made in an actual tandoor oven), are quite good for a free-on-a-ship casual eatery.

Pro tip: If you're sitting at one of the many tables scattered around Indulge Food Hall, you can order from any of the stands and counters via a tabletop tablet. But if you sit at the counter for any particular food outlet, you can only order from that outlet's menu. Pick your seats with that in mind.

A sleeper hit with no extra charge is The Local Bar and Grill, which has both indoor and outdoor seating with a casual diner vibe. It's open around the clock for table-served American comfort food (think: burgers, chicken wings and nachos). But most importantly, for me, it's a calmer and less crowded place for breakfast than the seemingly always-jammed buffet at the top of the ship (more on that in a moment). I loved sitting in its outdoor area on sea days, overlooking the water, for a leisurely eggs-bacon-and-toast breakfast served by a friendly waiter — a much more civilized experience than the buffet.

By contrast, the shiptop buffet called Surfside is an included-in-the-fare outlet to avoid. While a convenient quick-bite option for passengers lounging at the pool (it's right next door), it's too small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna. It has too few tables, too few food stations and too narrow a walkway along the food stations to be a pleasant experience much of the time it's open.

Rounding out the included-in-the-fare options are two larger complimentary sit-down restaurants, The Commodore Room and Hudson's. Both offer the same dinner menu, with decent, if not always consistent, offerings and pleasant service. Hudson's is also open for breakfast and lunch.

Among the upcharges at both eateries are $20-$30 fees for signature dishes from the ship's Cagney's Steakhouse, such as its ribeye steak ($25). While I'm generally not a fan of the trend toward more upcharges at supposedly included-in-the-fare cruise ship eateries, this does allow for what is one of my favorite dining hacks when sailing on a Norwegian ship: creating an almost-as-good-as-the-real-thing Cagney's steakhouse experience at less than half the price.

I order that ribeye and the always-available Caesar salad (nearly identical to the one at Cagney's except you don't get anchovies on top) and a couple of glasses of the included-in-Free-at-Sea-packages Malbec, which is the very same Malbec offered at Cagney's, and pretend I'm at the latter eatery. The total cost, including the mandatory gratuity, is $30 versus $72 per person at Cagney's.

No matter where you are on Norwegian Luna, you are never far from a bar. There are more than a dozen of them in the interior parts of the ship alone, plus more on the outside decks.

Among the liveliest (and my personal favorite) is the Metropolitan Bar, which stands out for its "zero waste" cocktails featuring such ingredients as syrup made from discarded banana peels. It's bustling every night with live music that ranges from Latin beats to classic '80s rock.

The Belvedere Bar at the top level of the atrium is also hopping with live music nightly, as is the Penrose Bar two decks below. (Musicians play at the base of the atrium not far from it.)

All three of these bars line high-traffic areas and can get busy. For something more tucked away, quieter and usually less crowded, the side-by-side Whiskey Bar and Swirl Wine Bar offer intimate spaces dedicated strictly to their respective namesake pours.

There's also the bar at The Local Bar & Grill mentioned in the restaurant section above, which serves as the casual go-to spot to catch a game over bar bites.

Beyond these, you'll find multiple bars servicing the pool and activity areas at the top of the ship as well as every interior entertainment venue, including the main theater and comedy club. Up at the very front of the ship, the Observation Lounge pairs a full bar with sweeping daytime ocean views.

What you won't find on Norwegian Luna, unlike on some competitor ships sailing from Miami, is a true craft cocktail venue. The Metropolitan Bar comes the closest with its "zero waste" cocktails. But even here, most drinks are quick-made affairs lacking the house-made ingredients, specialty clear ice and precision construction that has become commonplace at craft bars on land.

The Whiskey Bar also has craft elements, including a wide range of whiskeys and knowledgeable bartenders mixing old fashioneds, Boulevardiers and other whiskey drinks with precision. But the venue falls down on things like proper ice for drinks. (They oddly have just 20 large cubes available each night, which disappear fast, resulting in most cocktails coming out with the same small ice cubes found at the basic bars on the pool deck.)

For coffee drinkers, a full-size Starbucks in the atrium rounds out the beverage options.

Norwegian is no longer the leader in big ship entertainment, following cutbacks over the past three years. All the big-name Broadway shows, from "Jersey Boys" to "Kinky Boots," are gone. But it still offers solid entertainment in its main theaters, including the one on Norwegian Luna.

The big crowdpleaser on Norwegian Luna is "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John," a flashy tribute show that strings together John's biggest hits with visual pizzazz that includes elaborate costumes and choreography, special effects and archival footage projected on a back screen. If you're an Elton John fan like me, you'll love it.

The other big show in the Luna Theater, "HIKO: Innovation Meets Wonder," is a moody, sci-fi-themed mashup of custom-scored music, dance, showy costumes, 3D projections, lasers and acrobatics (think high-flying trampoline acts and aerial silk routines). It starts out slow but picks up toward the end.

There's also a rocking Eagles tribute show in the main theater with a full band, which is another crowd-pleaser. There are also more tribute shows focused on Billy Joel and Fleetwood Mac (the former in the smaller Syd Norman Pour House; the latter at the main theater).

And yes, you'll see a theme among the performers Norwegian has chosen for these tribute shows. These are all musical groups that are popular with Baby Boomers and Generation Xers who grew up with them, but have also had a resurgence among younger generations — perfect for Norwegian's wide demographic.

One other notable entertainment option is LunaTique Pop Circus, a bawdy, adults-only, cabaret-style nightlife experience set to pop music, with plenty of audience participation. (If the idea of being pulled up on stage terrifies you, don't sit in the front rows.) It's the only show on Norwegian Luna with an extra charge ($45 per person, including four drinks that get served to everyone as part of the show).

LunaTique Pop Circus takes place in Improv at Sea, an intimate comedy club that also is the place for stand-up comedy on most nights.

While not quite as elaborate as the entertainment on the larger Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises ships that sail out of Miami on weekends, the above shows have been earning high marks from cruisers since Norwegian Luna debuted and are among the most popular activities on the ship.

Just be warned that, because of that popularity, it can sometimes be hard to get a seat for these shows, which is a common complaint among passengers. With just 752 seats, the Luna Theater is small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna and fills up long before showtime. Ditto for the smaller Syd Norman's Pour House and Improv at Sea venues, which each can hold just 100 or so people.

If you want a seat for any of the shows, particularly a good seat near the front, head to the venue at least 45 minutes in advance.

Norwegian Luna has a lot to offer on its top decks, particularly in the "family fun" department.

The standout attraction is its giant Aqua Slidecoaster water ride. It uses the same magnetic accelerator system found in modern roller coasters to blast you skyward in a raft that then takes you winding back down a meandering waterslide course. It's both tons of fun and completely free.

You'll find several more fun family attractions tucked under and around the Aqua Slidecoaster, including a 12-hole, high-tech minigolf course where each stroke of your ball is electronically tracked and you get bonus points for hitting certain targets. It comes with a per-person charge of $5 but is well worth it.

Also in this area is The Stadium (free outdoor games including table tennis, bean bag toss and foosball) and the Bull's Eye Bar, which features tech-enhanced darts games.

You'll also find the entrance to The Drop, a terrifying-looking dry slide that spirals 10 decks down the side of the ship. It was a hard pass for me, but try it if you're daring.

Rounding out this area are a pickleball court and Glow Court — a high-tech sports court with an LED wall that lets you play challenging ball-throwing games (just be careful not to hit your partner with a ball, as I did; you might find yourself in the doghouse).

While great fun, these attractions eat up a lot of real estate on the top decks, leaving less room for pool areas. The ship's main pool area, just in front of the Aqua Slidecoaster, feels small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna (and, indeed, was uncomfortably jammed on sea days during my sailing).

One deck up from the pool is the often-crowded Kids' Aqua Park, where little ones can enjoy water sprayers and mini waterslides.

The solution to escape the crowds (if you're kid-free, at least) is to spend $289 per person for a weekly pass to the adults-only Vibe Beach Club — a separate, keycard-access-only deck-top lounge area that is roughly the same size as the main pool area but limited to just 166 passengers. It is blissfully uncrowded and quiet compared to the main pool area and has its own bar and hot tubs facing the sea.

Pro tip: Splurge for one of the 12 private cabanas at the Vibe Beach Club, which cost a seemingly high $619 per week but come with access for two people, so they're really only about $310 per person. That's just $21 more per person than buying two Vibe passes, and it's a much nicer experience.

Alternatively, you can book a cabin in The Haven, which, as noted above, also has its own decktop lounge area (at the back of the ship) with its own pool and bar.

Between these two areas (Vibe and The Haven), Norwegian Luna notably has a lot more of its decktop real estate devoted to exclusive upcharge areas than other big ships sailing from Miami. What this effectively means is that the ship offers a bifurcated decktop experience. If you pay up, you will experience something more relaxing and exclusive than you will find on many other big ships. If you don't, the top deck experience might feel less appealing.

That said, if you're willing to head down nine decks, you'll find additional outdoor lounge space with lounge chairs and small plunge pools along an outdoor promenade that wraps around the sides of the ships. With a cool South Beach vibe that includes plush circular seats for two surrounded by wading pools, it's an innovative additional outdoor area that is often less crowded than the top-deck pool area.

For indoor fun, the family-focused Luna Game Zone near the Observation Lounge offers an array of video, virtual reality and other games (some for free and some for a fee). Plus, for adults, there's a sizable casino with VIP and smoking rooms, as well as slots and table games.

Norwegian Luna also has a massive, multilevel spa (the Mandara Spa) with one of the loveliest and most relaxing thermal suites at sea. Accessible for an extra charge, it has a stunning, two-deck-high room with water therapy pools; a separate area that is home to all sorts of therapeutic rooms including Finnish, charcoal and clay saunas, a steam room and a salt room; and a separate, blissfully relaxing room full of heated loungers overlooking the sea.

Just be warned that access to the thermal suite costs a sky-high $630 per person for the week (though discounts are sometimes available onboard at the start of the cruise).

The spa area is also where you'll find the ship's fitness room, which is free to use and offers plenty of cardio equipment and free weights, but lacks a full range of weight machines.

The ship's entertainment staff also programs all sorts of daily activities throughout the ship, including trivia games, karaoke, art and dance classes, and family events.

Through at least April 2028, Norwegian Luna will mostly sail seven-night cruises from Miami to the Caribbean, with departures on Saturdays. The exception is during the summer of 2027, when it will reposition to New York for four-, five- and seven-night cruises to Bermuda.

When sailing from Miami, the ship operates both Eastern and Western Caribbean itineraries. Eastern Caribbean itineraries typically include stops at Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic; St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands; Tortola, British Virgin Islands; and Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas. Western Caribbean itineraries typically bring calls in Roatan, Honduras; Harvest Caye, Belize; and Costa Maya and Cozumel, Mexico.

Related: Eastern Caribbean vs. Western Caribbean cruises

Fares for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $549 per person, based on double occupancy. Fares for seven-night Bermuda sailings start at $1,229 per person, based on double occupancy.

Such pricing is for inside cabins on the most offseason dates. You'll pay more for oceanview and balcony cabins and suites, as well as for sailings on more in-demand weeks.

Norwegian Luna is a big new ship that feels more refined and upscale than many of the other big new ships sailing out of Miami. That's in part because of its more elegant design and its (relatively) smaller size. The downside of that smaller size is that the ship doesn't have quite as many onboard attractions — like decktop features, showrooms, restaurants and bars — as some of its competitors.

#6030. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6029. Airbnb Rates Rose After California Required Upfront Pricing—Research Shows Guests Still Benefit

California required Airbnb to put mandatory fees into the price travelers see up front. A new study of San Francisco and San Diego listings finds rates rose 4.8% relative to cities outside the mandate. The researchers still conclude guests came out ahead. Being able to figure out what you’re buying has value. A cheaper-looking listing isn’t necessarily a cheaper stay. The rental with the lowest headline price isn’t necessarily the one you’d choose if you could compare them properly. Back in 2022, when Airbnb introduced a toggle to show the price including fees, I wrote that guests shouldn’t have to turn it on. Showing what a stay costs ought to be the default. (And why would you toggle it off except for research purposes?) Ultimately hiding charges punishes honest businesses. The property showing its full price looks more expensive than the competitor holding something back until later. You make the customer click through every listing and do the math just to find out what a property costs, which makes it costly to compare. I’ve even covered a rental on Booking.com with a $1,000 destination fee, on top of a resort fee and cleaning fee – listed in the fine print. The Fees Became Easier To See. The Stays Didn’t Get Cheaper. The November working paper compares entire-home listings in the two California cities with matched properties in Seattle and Chicago, using July 2023–July 2025 data. Its price measure includes cleaning charges, but excludes Airbnb’s service fee and taxes. Listings more dependent on cleaning fees as a portion of total price were more likely to exit the platform. Higher quality listings were more likely to remain, while new listings offered lower fees and prices than incumbents. That creates an opportunity for hosts who were already offering a good deal. If you build cleaning into your rate while the place next door breaks it out, your property can look overpriced. Put both totals on the screen and you may be able to charge a higher rate while still offering a lower total price than competitors. There can also be fewer rentals competing for the same guests if enough hosts leave. That’s a reason not to assume that forcing everyone to advertise total price will lower prices. Limits To The Model Holding the available properties fixed, the paper’s model finds higher prices more than wipe out the direct gains from disclosure. Changes in the rental pool flip the result positive. Hotels aren’t included. Excluding storm-affected comparison months also reduces the estimated rate increase to 2.9%. Someone returning to the same property at a higher price might be worse off. Someone who avoids a bad value rental, or finds a better one once the prices are comparable, can benefit even while spending more. If an Airbnb becomes too expensive, the alternative isn’t necessarily another vacation rental. It might be a hotel, a different neighborhood, or deciding not to take the trip. The model also leaves out time saved searching. Anyone who’s clicked through 20 listings just to assemble a usable set of prices knows that’s worth something, too. The estimate of how much better off people are takes more assumptions than observing what happened to rates. A Cleaning Cost Can Be Real Without Being A Surprise Cleaning a house after a two night stay can cost about as much as cleaning it after a week. There’s a reason longer stays can be cheaper per night. Showing the full price doesn’t stop a host from accounting for that. Say one property charges $150 a night plus $150 for cleaning. Another charges $210 a night with cleaning included. For two nights, the first costs $450 and the second $420, before other charges. For a week, the first is cheaper. A search where you’ve already entered your dates can show the right comparison without making you calculate it yourself. Airbnb finally made total price display standard worldwide in April 2025, generally before taxes. The study looks back at California moving earlier to help understand the effect of the change. I’ve rented homes on Martha’s Vineyard and when visiting family outside Australia’s Gold Coast. A whole house can make more sense than hotel rooms for a family or group. Airbnb also now even says that the cleaning fee actually buys the cleaning, limiting the chores hosts can require. I once paid $300 a night for an Airbnb with a locked plastic box over the thermostat. You still have to be careful out there! The November working paper compares entire-home listings in the two California cities with matched properties in Seattle and Chicago, using July 2023–July 2025 data. Its price measure includes cleaning charges, but excludes Airbnb’s service fee and taxes. Listings more dependent on cleaning fees as a portion of total price were more likely to exit the platform. Higher quality listings were more likely to remain, while new listings offered lower fees and prices than incumbents. That creates an opportunity for hosts who were already offering a good deal. If you build cleaning into your rate while the place next door breaks it out, your property can look overpriced. Put both totals on the screen and you may be able to charge a higher rate while still offering a lower total price than competitors. There can also be fewer rentals competing for the same guests if enough hosts leave. That’s a reason not to assume that forcing everyone to advertise total price will lower prices. Limits To The Model Holding the available properties fixed, the paper’s model finds higher prices more than wipe out the direct gains from disclosure. Changes in the rental pool flip the result positive. Hotels aren’t included. Excluding storm-affected comparison months also reduces the estimated rate increase to 2.9%. Someone returning to the same property at a higher price might be worse off. Someone who avoids a bad value rental, or finds a better one once the prices are comparable, can benefit even while spending more. If an Airbnb becomes too expensive, the alternative isn’t necessarily another vacation rental. It might be a hotel, a different neighborhood, or deciding not to take the trip. The model also leaves out time saved searching. Anyone who’s clicked through 20 listings just to assemble a usable set of prices knows that’s worth something, too. The estimate of how much better off people are takes more assumptions than observing what happened to rates. A Cleaning Cost Can Be Real Without Being A Surprise Cleaning a house after a two night stay can cost about as much as cleaning it after a week. There’s a reason longer stays can be cheaper per night. Showing the full price doesn’t stop a host from accounting for that. Say one property charges $150 a night plus $150 for cleaning. Another charges $210 a night with cleaning included. For two nights, the first costs $450 and the second $420, before other charges. For a week, the first is cheaper. A search where you’ve already entered your dates can show the right comparison without making you calculate it yourself. Airbnb finally made total price display standard worldwide in April 2025, generally before taxes. The study looks back at California moving earlier to help understand the effect of the change. I’ve rented homes on Martha’s Vineyard and when visiting family outside Australia’s Gold Coast. A whole house can make more sense than hotel rooms for a family or group. Airbnb also now even says that the cleaning fee actually buys the cleaning, limiting the chores hosts can require. I once paid $300 a night for an Airbnb with a locked plastic box over the thermostat. You still have to be careful out there! #6028. Elon Musk Owes South Africa Nothing

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa (left) and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk

Last week, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived in Silicon Valley seeking investment. He also had a message for Elon Musk: Remember your South African roots and “give back.”

It is an extraordinary appeal from the leader of a country crippled by unemployment, corruption, and economic stagnation. His African National Congress bears most of the responsibility. Yet Ramaphosa came to America, begging bowl in hand, asking successful entrepreneurs to help repair the damage. His government, meanwhile, obstructs one of the most obvious ways Musk could help — allowing Starlink to operate in South Africa.

#6026. American Airlines Passengers Restrain Man Who Went For The Door As Flight Attendant Blocks Him With A Drink Cart

Sean Bennett was asleep a few rows back on American Airlines’ San Diego–Chicago redeye when he heard a flight attendant yelling for a man to get away from the door. Passengers rushed up front to help. A second witness says a flight attendant pushed a drink cart up the aisle to keep the struggle from spilling back into the cabin. Bennett posted several videos from his seat. People crowded into the forward galley and got zip ties around the man’s wrists as he kept resisting almost until they landed. American Airlines flight 1494 took off from San Diego at 10:53 p.m. Pacific on Tuesday, November 24. About 40 minutes later, up at around 34,000 feet, it turned right for Phoenix. Police say the man had left his seat, walked to the front and repeatedly ignored instructions to sit back down. Passengers thought the man was trying to “take over the plane.” One report says he went for the cockpit door, but pilots told American’s operations center the man “tried to open the cabin door.” This was reported as a Level 3 threat which means life-threatening behavior. An attempt to breach the cockpit is Level 4. The man wound up on the ground in his underwear in the galley. At altitude, cabin pressure holds an exterior door shut. The Asiana Airlines passenger who actually opened an Airbus A321 exit was able to do it because the aircraft had descended enough on final approach. On another American flight to Chicago in 2024, Zach Etkind (‘the Wonton Don’) and five other passengers wrestled a man into the aisle after he went for an exit. They used duct tape and flex cuffs and the pilots went back to Albuquerque. This time the Airbus A321 landed in Phoenix around 1 a.m. Wednesday morning. Police met it at the gate. The man went to the hospital with a minor injury. The passenger who shared video of the inflight incident reports that he was upgraded on his next connection. Bennett posted several videos from his seat. People crowded into the forward galley and got zip ties around the man’s wrists as he kept resisting almost until they landed.

American Airlines flight 1494 took off from San Diego at 10:53 p.m. Pacific on Tuesday, November 24. About 40 minutes later, up at around 34,000 feet, it turned right for Phoenix. Police say the man had left his seat, walked to the front and repeatedly ignored instructions to sit back down.

Passengers thought the man was trying to “take over the plane.” One report says he went for the cockpit door, but pilots told American’s operations center the man “tried to open the cabin door.”

This was reported as a Level 3 threat which means life-threatening behavior. An attempt to breach the cockpit is Level 4. The man wound up on the ground in his underwear in the galley.

At altitude, cabin pressure holds an exterior door shut. The Asiana Airlines passenger who actually opened an Airbus A321 exit was able to do it because the aircraft had descended enough on final approach.

On another American flight to Chicago in 2024, Zach Etkind (‘the Wonton Don’) and five other passengers wrestled a man into the aisle after he went for an exit. They used duct tape and flex cuffs and the pilots went back to Albuquerque.

This time the Airbus A321 landed in Phoenix around 1 a.m. Wednesday morning. Police met it at the gate. The man went to the hospital with a minor injury.

#6025. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6024. Bilt Palladium Is My Best Card For Everyday Spending—Get It By December 31 To Lock In Its Most Valuable Rewards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Bilt is changing how its credit cards earn rewards, and cardholders who want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash on everyday spending need to make a choice. I’ve already opted to keep the benefit—it’s a big reason my Bilt Palladium gets most of my spending.

If you don’t have a Bilt card, I’d get one now. You need to apply, get approved and accept the card offer by December 31, 2026 to preserve the choice of earning 4% Bilt Cash. Existing cardmembers also need to actively choose to keep it before their first card anniversary in 2027. Doing nothing means moving into the new rewards structure.

The Bilt Palladium Card gets the majority of my spending. I pay my mortgage through Bilt, but the card would be valuable to me even without a housing payment that can earn points.

I’ve written that Palladium looks complicated, but it’s the best everyday rewards card.

I consider these the most valuable points. You can redeem them at 1.25 cents apiece through Bilt’s travel portal, but I usually want to transfer them. The transfer partner lineup gives me access to:

Most transfers are 1:1. Accor is 3:2, I Prefer is 1:2, and Amtrak is 2:1. Bilt also runs large Rent Day transfer bonuses, often with better offers for higher elite tiers. I’ve used bonuses for transfers to Japan Airlines, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic and Air France KLM. Earning points quickly and then transferring with a bonus is why I want so much of my spending here.

Bilt is changing the earning choice in 2027. Today, cardmembers can choose:

Most cardmembers already choose the second option. Palladium is still a great card that way. But for most people putting significant spending on the card, especially when they’re generating more Bilt Cash than their housing payments would consume, I think the 4% option is much more valuable. Once you’ve reached the highest housing multiplier, spending more doesn’t increase that multiplier. With Flexible Bilt Cash, more spending keeps producing more Bilt Cash to use.

There are exceptions. I’ve explained how the housing option can produce an effective 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. At the 25% spending threshold, $1,000 of everyday spending and $4,000 of eligible housing payments earn 2,000 points from the purchases and 2,000 from housing. That’s 4,000 points against $1,000 of everyday spending. The relationship between your spending and housing payments determines which choice works best.

For me, the accelerators alone are a reason to preserve Bilt Cash earning. Spend $200 in Bilt Cash to activate one and you earn an extra point per dollar on the next $5,000 in eligible spending. Palladium’s 2X becomes 3X. That $5,000 also generates another $200 Bilt Cash, which can fund the next accelerator. Each eligible cardholder can activate five per calendar year.

My wife and I have both maxed out our accelerators this year: 3 points per dollar on $50,000 of combined spending. We’ve earned points on housing payments as well.

She has an authorized user card on my Palladium account. It costs $95 annually and comes with her own Priority Pass membership. She doesn’t receive a second set of my annual hotel and Bilt Cash credits, but she can earn rewards in her own Bilt account (or I can switch it to mine).

I’ve laid out how my wife and I use this. I directed the points and Bilt Cash from her spending into her account instead of mine. She earns her own status, funds her own accelerators, and can take advantage of transfer bonuses separately. When an offer bonuses transfers of up to 100,000 Bilt Points per member, two accounts give us room to bonus 200,000 points, with each person’s bonus determined by their own status.

An authorized user’s spending doesn’t automatically get the primary cardholder’s active accelerator. They need to activate their own, using their own Bilt Cash. Bilt also gives the primary cardholder separate card numbers and controls over authorized user spending, including transaction and monthly limits. You can add an authorized user starting at age 13. But for my wife and me, the separate rewards accounts are the reason this has been so useful.

And I’ve gotten far more out of Bilt Cash than just faster points earning. I’ve redeemed it for:

For my everyday spending, Palladium earns the points I want faster than any other card, and the benefits have been incredible. The new structure still allows Palladium and Obsidian cardmembers to use accelerators. Palladium’s $400 annual hotel credit and $200 annual Bilt Cash become a $600 annual Bilt Cash deposit at the card anniversary. That can fund three accelerators. Members can also earn Bilt Cash from other activity, including $50 for each 25,000 qualifying points. But they won’t replenish it at 4% of everyday spending.

Keeping the existing structure also preserves my separate $200 hotel credits, which I can stack with Bilt Cash hotel redemptions. The Bilt Cash hotel redemption allowance moves from monthly to twice yearly starting January 1 even for those keeping 4% earning, but I can still get the two $300 discounts this way.

Plus, Bilt Cash now expires at the end of the month 12 months after it’s earned. Cash earned in February 2026 lasts through February 28, 2027. The old rule would have wiped out everything over $100 at year-end. Having more time to use what I earn makes the 4% option better for me.

If you don’t have a card, I’d apply now and complete approval and acceptance before December 31. My choice is Bilt Palladium. The ability to preserve 4% Bilt Cash also applies to the Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) and no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (See rates and fees).

And if you already have a card, don’t assume your current selection of Flexible Bilt Cash protects you from the change. You need to proactively choose to keep it. I’ve already done this:

The new rewards model is selected by default.

You have until your first card anniversary in 2027 to make that election. Preserve it now and you can still move to the new structure later. Once that switch takes effect, you can’t move back. That’s why getting a Bilt Palladium Card now makes so much sense – keeping the earning option. They’ll pry the 4% Bilt Cash earning option from my cold, dead hands, as they say.

#6023. How Long Can Jensen Huang and Nvidia Defy Gravity?

His reinstatement at Trump’s urging is a perilous high-wire act.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks at the annual Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, Nev., January 6, 2026.

It’s foolish to be astonished by anything anymore. Still, Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer, just eleven days after his resignation and six days after the board of directors said it had no intention to reinstate him, is surprising, to say the least.

The Wall Street Journal reports Nvidia’s statement that the board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” and is “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Andrew C. McCarthy is a senior fellow at National Review Institute, an NR contributing editor, and author of Ball of Collusion: The Plot to Rig an Election and Destroy a Presidency.

#6022. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6021. American Airlines May Hire A CEO Successor To Robert Isom Before End Of Year — Its Best Outside Candidate Is At Southwest

When Robert Isom became CEO of American Airlines in 2022, he never named another executive to replace him as president. Now former Wall Street Journal airline reporter Scott McCartney says conversations he’s had lead him to think “American is trying to bring in an outsider as president and heir apparent to CEO Robert Isom.” And he thinks a president could be named by year-end. That’s much more plausible than long-reported speculation that Isom would get replaced as CEO by the board. On Airlines Confidential, McCartney thinks Isom wants to turn American around and then hand it off. McCartney’s first suggestion is a good one: drive across town and talk to Southwest’s COO Andrew Watterson who’s reportedly been sidelined from the CEO path there. American existing chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, has already appeared to play much of the President role (albeit without full reporting lines tiering up to him). A New President Lets American ‘Try Before They Buy’ This is the board that watched Delta take American’s South American partner LATAM away from it in 2019. Doug Parker kept his job for another two and a half years. When he handed it to Isom, he stayed on as chairman. A board with that history can get comfortable with succession planning a lot more easily than with removing a CEO for poor performance. And – for all of the lingering complaints about Robert Isom – they’ve finally been turning around the airline’s value proposition. Vice Chair Steve Johnson, who ran commercial for 18 months after Vasu Raja left and oversaw the new Citi deal, retires at year-end. Chief Operating Officer David Seymour never got Isom’s old President job and is retiring with severance. Hiring a president lets the board try before it buys. Someone who has run a much smaller airline can be a credible candidate for this job even if you wouldn’t hand them American right away. But what portfolio would the president have? Isom just told employees that Seymour’s successor, JonCarlo Gulbranson, will report directly to him. He could change his mind. Nat Pieper Has Already Been Doing Much Of The Job McCartney says he’s hearing that American wants someone with Delta experience and nobody inside is ready yet. The first requirement would hardly rule out Pieper. Pieper ran Delta’s commercial business in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and India. He helped bring Alaska into oneworld and went on to run the alliance. He’s only been at American about a year, so still qualifies as an outsider. He’s the one explaining to employees why American has to fight United in Chicago. On the October earnings call, Pieper took analysts’ questions and walked investors through an 18.5% year-over-year increase in premium unit revenue. After the August reorganization, Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden reports to him alone, rather than jointly to him and the operating head. He’s led the process to purchase new widebody jets that’s expected to come to completion soon. None of that is unusual for a commercial chief, but in front of employees and investors he’s already doing much of a president’s job. You can see why Pieper’s name was already coming up around headquarters in February. He’s the only plausible internal successor today. The next step would be greater operational responsibility, and a greater role in finance. Who Would Be Worth Hiring From The Outside? Southwest COO Andrew Watterson wouldn’t even need to relocated, and he’s served as that airline’s chief commercial officer as well. He had responsibility for revenue for two years while running the operation. He’s had to both sell the schedule and run the flights. And he’s well-liked by employees. Paul Jacobson is McCartney’s other suggestion. If he gets passed over for Mary Barra’s job as CEO of General Motors, he could be available. Jacobson spent 23 years at Delta, from financial analyst to CFO. His team raised nearly $30 billion during the pandemic. American has plenty of debt, but its bigger problem is getting customers to pay a premium to fly it. While Delta did this, Jacobson wasn’t in charge of commercial or operations. And he already makes as much as Isom does. Contra McCartney, I’d put Peter Ingram ahead of Jude Bricker. McCartney mentions both, and both spent time at American. Ingram was Hawaiian’s CFO, commercial head and then CEO. He couldn’t turn Hawaiian around and sold it to American, but he wouldn’t be asked to become CEO on day one. And he ran a premium global airline, albeit a smaller one. Bricker was president of Allegiant Air, then ran Sun Country. He also took first class out of Sun Country’s planes. That may have been the right call for Sun Country but his record is running cost-focused operations, while American’s challenges are primarily around revenue rather than cost. Besides, Bricker just bought into Omni Air and became its CEO this month. He’d have to walk away from his own deal. The Delta executive I’d want is Glen Hauenstein. He spent nearly a decade as Delta’s president building precisely the premium revenue advantage American wants. He never got the CEO chair there. But he retired as president in February and agreed to advise Delta through year-end. But it’s not clear he’d come out of retirement for another president’s job without a date for the handover, and he’s older than Jacobson. I wasn’t a fan of Hauenstein, but he certainly understands the commercial side of the Delta business. However Hauenstein is not going to happen. His Delta non-compete appears to run through the end of 2028. Hauenstein retired as president on February 28, 2026. The agreement runs two years, but he’s continuing to receive payments as an advisor through the end of 2026. And Delta’s compensation plan specifically says that continuing to provide services as an independent contractor keeps the clock from starting unless the compensation committee decides otherwise. American Airlines is explicitly named in the non-compete, Hauenstein would lose his outstanding incentive awards, and the agreement lets Delta seek an injunction to stop him from taking the job. At Delta’s current share price, Hauenstein has an estimated $20 million in unvested incentives contingent on honoring non-compete (if Delta hits its targets). After the next round of payouts, that falls to $7.5 million. American could offer to make him whole, but they still risk a court enforcing the non-compete via an injunction to stop the hire. McCartney wonders whether the CEO search at GM was even triggered by American’s interest in Jacobson – deciding whether they want to give him the big chair or let him go. And McCartney gives long odds to another Delta alumnus, former operating head Jim Whitehurst, who is now a senior partner at Silver Lake and a United board member. There’s a cost to hiring any of them over Pieper. In 2016 American chose then-COO Isom for president and American’s President Scott Kirby went to United. Parker later told employees the board didn’t think it could keep both men, and they had to choose. Ten years later, the executive American is counting on to beat Kirby in Chicago is Nat Pieper. In deciding whether to hire him a new boss, the board has another moment of choosing. None of that is unusual for a commercial chief, but in front of employees and investors he’s already doing much of a president’s job. You can see why Pieper’s name was already coming up around headquarters in February. He’s the only plausible internal successor today. The next step would be greater operational responsibility, and a greater role in finance. Who Would Be Worth Hiring From The Outside? Southwest COO Andrew Watterson wouldn’t even need to relocated, and he’s served as that airline’s chief commercial officer as well. He had responsibility for revenue for two years while running the operation. He’s had to both sell the schedule and run the flights. And he’s well-liked by employees. Paul Jacobson is McCartney’s other suggestion. If he gets passed over for Mary Barra’s job as CEO of General Motors, he could be available. Jacobson spent 23 years at Delta, from financial analyst to CFO. His team raised nearly $30 billion during the pandemic. American has plenty of debt, but its bigger problem is getting customers to pay a premium to fly it. While Delta did this, Jacobson wasn’t in charge of commercial or operations. And he already makes as much as Isom does. Contra McCartney, I’d put Peter Ingram ahead of Jude Bricker. McCartney mentions both, and both spent time at American. Ingram was Hawaiian’s CFO, commercial head and then CEO. He couldn’t turn Hawaiian around and sold it to American, but he wouldn’t be asked to become CEO on day one. And he ran a premium global airline, albeit a smaller one. Bricker was president of Allegiant Air, then ran Sun Country. He also took first class out of Sun Country’s planes. That may have been the right call for Sun Country but his record is running cost-focused operations, while American’s challenges are primarily around revenue rather than cost. Besides, Bricker just bought into Omni Air and became its CEO this month. He’d have to walk away from his own deal. The Delta executive I’d want is Glen Hauenstein. He spent nearly a decade as Delta’s president building precisely the premium revenue advantage American wants. He never got the CEO chair there. But he retired as president in February and agreed to advise Delta through year-end. But it’s not clear he’d come out of retirement for another president’s job without a date for the handover, and he’s older than Jacobson. I wasn’t a fan of Hauenstein, but he certainly understands the commercial side of the Delta business. However Hauenstein is not going to happen. His Delta non-compete appears to run through the end of 2028. Hauenstein retired as president on February 28, 2026. The agreement runs two years, but he’s continuing to receive payments as an advisor through the end of 2026. And Delta’s compensation plan specifically says that continuing to provide services as an independent contractor keeps the clock from starting unless the compensation committee decides otherwise. American Airlines is explicitly named in the non-compete, Hauenstein would lose his outstanding incentive awards, and the agreement lets Delta seek an injunction to stop him from taking the job. At Delta’s current share price, Hauenstein has an estimated $20 million in unvested incentives contingent on honoring non-compete (if Delta hits its targets). After the next round of payouts, that falls to $7.5 million. American could offer to make him whole, but they still risk a court enforcing the non-compete via an injunction to stop the hire. McCartney wonders whether the CEO search at GM was even triggered by American’s interest in Jacobson – deciding whether they want to give him the big chair or let him go. And McCartney gives long odds to another Delta alumnus, former operating head Jim Whitehurst, who is now a senior partner at Silver Lake and a United board member. There’s a cost to hiring any of them over Pieper. In 2016 American chose then-COO Isom for president and American’s President Scott Kirby went to United. Parker later told employees the board didn’t think it could keep both men, and they had to choose. Ten years later, the executive American is counting on to beat Kirby in Chicago is Nat Pieper. In deciding whether to hire him a new boss, the board has another moment of choosing. Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. More About Gary »

I want flights that run on time without mechanical delays. Currently that seems to be impossible

It comes down to how best to deal with 2 existential crisis at AA:

1. Their dreadful finances 2. A workforce that understandably hates their lives

To consistently charge a premium that actually generates a profit, AA must solve both problems.

We can rely on the AA board to screw this up too! Parker’s hand-picked lap dogs haven’t made a decision since the merger in 2013. They are there for the benefits. Any real board would have ousted a CEO after the third DUI but Parker treated them to lifetime first class so he could have golf and drinking buddies. And deer in the headlights Isom has never had an original thought and is so insecure that he visibly shakes whenever Kirby speaks and he thinks innovation means copying 10 year old ideas. Small wonder AA sucks.

I feel like AA hired Isom’s successor a year ago – Nate Pieper. He’s been acting like the defacto CEO since that time. I feel like the last year has been the ‘try/buy’ period…the President title ought to come in the new year to make the succession plan obvious and public. It seems most public articulation of strategy in the last year has not come from Isom but rather from Pieper. Isom has seemed more of a pending emeritus exec than an actual leader. I suspect we’ll hear something by the start of Q2. I personally don’t see how bringing in a Hawaiian, Allegiant or Southwest exec have any experience nor relevance to what AA must do moving forward.
