Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 100,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Delta Air Lines and American Express offer seven cobranded cards for everyone from occasional Delta flyers to frequent travelers.

Depending on the card and the offer you qualify for, you could earn thousands of bonus Delta SkyMiles.

Here’s how the current offers compare and what to consider before applying.

Apply for the : Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The following is a comparison of the various welcome offers currently available. Note that TPG values Delta SkyMiles at 1.2 cents per mile as of November 2026. This valuation assumes you're using your miles to book flights with Delta or one of its partners.

American Express has a few eligibility rules to keep in mind before applying for one of these cards. For starters, Amex typically only allows a person to earn one welcome bonus per card in their lifetime. That means you'll want to prioritize applying when a card offers an elevated, limited-time offer, such as the ones all but one of these cards have right now.

You also may not be eligible for a welcome bonus on a personal Delta Amex card if you have or previously had a higher-tier Delta Amex card. For example, if you have or previously had the Delta Reserve Amex, you may not be eligible for the welcome offers on the Delta Blue, the Delta Gold and the Delta Platinum.

Delta's business Amex cards are not subject to this same "family rule."

Amex may consider other factors, including your income, your credit score and your history with the issuer, when determining your eligibility. Fortunately, you'll generally find out whether you're eligible for a welcome offer before accepting the card.

Related: A complete guide to Amex's 1-bonus-per-lifetime restrictions

Delta offers four personal cards. The card that is right for you depends on how frequently you fly with Delta and how much you’re willing to pay for an annual fee.

Let’s take a look at what differentiates each of the Delta SkyMiles personal cards.

Best for: Delta loyalists or those who want Sky Club access (subject to limitations).

The is ideal for hardcore Delta fans and frequent flyers.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

This bonus is worth up to $1,500, per our valuations.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this is an excellent time to apply. It matches the highest mileage bonus we’ve seen on the card and requires $1,000 less in spending than the previous 125,000-mile offer with the lowest spending requirement.

Key benefits: Delta’s premium consumer credit card offers a range of valuable perks. For loyal Delta flyers who enjoy visiting the Sky Club, this card can pay for itself through lounge access, spending boosts and other benefits. If you're chasing status with Delta, the Delta Reserve's Medallion Qualification Dollar head start and earning boost make it a very compelling option.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Plus, you'll enjoy a slew of Delta-related perks, including:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve.

If you fly frequently with Delta but can’t justify the pricier Delta SkyMiles Reserve, the is worth considering.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 90,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,080.

If you qualify for the full 90,000 miles, this is a strong offer for $3,000 in spending. We’ve seen offers with more miles or a statement credit, though they required more spending.

Key benefits: This card is a good option if you fly Delta regularly and want to earn miles on purchases and reach elite status. The Delta Platinum is a good choice for status chasers who want an extra boost but don't want to pay the Delta Reserve's steep price tag.

However, even if you aren’t pursuing status, the companion certificate alone can make the annual fee for this card worth it.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum.

Best for: Occasional Delta flyers or those test-driving a Delta card.

If you want to take advantage of a welcome bonus but don’t fly Delta frequently, the is a strong option.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 80,000 bonus miles after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

TPG's valuations place this bonus at up to $960.

If you qualify for the full 80,000 miles, now is a good time to apply. However, we have seen up to 90,000 miles — as well as up to 80,000 miles plus a statement credit — offered before.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150.

Key benefits: This card is ideal for occasional Delta flyers seeking a few extra perks when flying with the airline.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold.

If you want an entry-level card to start earning SkyMiles and fly less frequently with Delta, then the is the card for you.

Current welcome offer: Earn 10,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, these miles are worth $120. The SkyMiles Blue typically doesn't receive an elevated offer, so we recommend applying whenever you're ready.

Key benefits: As a no-annual-fee card, it offers fewer benefits than the others. Still, there are some simple perks for cardmembers.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Blue.

If you own a small business or have a side hustle through which you pay business expenses, one of these offers may be a great addition to your work wallet.

Best for: Business owners who fly Delta frequently and want lounge access.

As the most expensive business card Delta offers, the comes packed with great perks for Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,500.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this clears our usual threshold. The highest offer we’ve seen was 200,000 miles after $20,000 in spending, compared with $15,000 for this offer.

Key benefits: This card offers a range of useful perks for Delta-loyal small-business owners. For small-business owners looking to achieve status with Delta, this card is the best option available.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on purchases made directly with Delta.

Its suite of Delta-related benefits includes:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business.

Best for: Business owners who fly frequently with Delta.

Business owners who are looking for a good mid-tier airline business card should consider the for its earning potential and benefits.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

According to TPG's valuations, this offer is worth up to $1,200.

The full 100,000-mile bonus matches the highest mileage offer we’ve seen, though previous offers awarded the same bonus after $8,000 in purchases. If you already have $10,000 in eligible business spending planned and want the card now, this is a good offer. If you’re flexible on timing, we’d consider waiting for the same bonus with a lower spending requirement.

Key benefits: This is a solid mid-tier option for business owners who travel with Delta semifrequently. If you want elite status with Delta but don't want to pay the Delta Reserve Business' high annual fee, this is your next best option.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business.

Best for: Business owners who fly occasionally with Delta.

The is ideal for smaller businesses or business owners who aren’t Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 85,000 bonus miles after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The bonus is worth up to $1,020 when factoring in TPG's valuations.

If you qualify for all 85,000 miles, this is a good time to apply. It’s just 5,000 miles shy of the highest offer we’ve seen, which also required $6,000 in spending. If the card already fits your business, we’d take the full offer.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150.

Key benefits: Even if they don't fly Delta often, small-business owners can still benefit from this card's perks.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Business.

With a full lineup of Delta cards, you may wonder how to pick the best offer for your needs. While it might be tempting to go with the highest offer, you should also consider its long-term value to your wallet.

The good news is that many of these offers can be a great fit, depending on your travel habits. As a roundup:

Related: Why the Delta SkyMiles Reserve card is still one of the best cards in my wallet

Delta and American Express offer a wide range of cobranded cards, whether you fly with the airline occasionally or are a Delta loyalist.

Just remember that American Express has a once-per-card-per-lifetime rule for welcome offers. If you've had a particular Delta Amex before or, in some cases, a higher-tier personal Delta card, you may not be eligible for that card's welcome offer.

Welcome offers vary, so check the bonus you’re offered and make sure you can meet the spending requirement with purchases you already plan to make.

#6019. American Airlines Pilots And Flight Attendants Unite To Demand New Leadership—Say They’re Done Asking Management To Do Better

Five days after American Airlines announced it was replacing Chief Operating Officer, the flight attendants and pilots unions say that change at the top needs to go further. And they’re making this case in part based on American’s poor recovery from this month’s FAA nationwide ground stop. Captain Nick Silva of the Allied Pilots Association and Julie Hedrick of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants signed a joint letter that both unions sent out. They tell management, “We have spent years asking you to do better. Those days are over.” A few lines later they say what they want. “American Airlines needs a new direction — and leadership capable of delivering it.”

Captain Nick Silva of the Allied Pilots Association and Julie Hedrick of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants signed a joint letter that both unions sent out. They tell management, “We have spent years asking you to do better. Those days are over.” A few lines later they say what they want.

“American Airlines needs a new direction — and leadership capable of delivering it.”

In February, the flight attendants’ union board voted unanimously that it had no confidence in Robert Isom. Pilots did not go as far.

And today’s note is being misinterpreted by some as a call for Isom to go. Today’s letter leaves his name out of it, never naming him at all. It’s actually a weaker call than they made earlier in the year.

This gives the unions room to claim a win even if Isom stays CEO. As I wrote earlier today, American may be looking for an outside president who could eventually succeed Isom, and former Wall Street Journal airline reporter Scott McCartney says a hire could come by year-end.

The unions circulated FlightAware data compiled by BofA Global Research. On Saturday, American canceled 42% of its mainline flights, Delta 28% and United 26%. By Sunday, Delta was down to 5%. However, The chart is misleading by picking only two U.S. airlines and mainline flights only. JetBlue cancelled 44% of flights over the 3 days. They left JetBlue off the chart. Including regional flights, American, United and Delta all performed similarly – American cancelled 28.5%, Delta 25.1%, and United 23%. So the union heads are cherry picking by focusing only on mainline. (American even owns three of its regional carriers.) After Winter Storm Fern at the start of the year, I obtained minutes from a flight attendants’ union executive committee meeting. Hedrick said American sent crews to a service center that couldn’t actually book hotel rooms. What struck me at the time was how much sympathy she had for management. On November 15, her union reported that flight attendants waited hours to get their trip assignments fixed, then waited again for rooms. Some never got one. American needed those same people rested to fly passengers the next day. The unions take a swipe in their note at American investing in better seats and lounges. They need those to generate more revenue. Silva himself said in September he wished American had started investing in customers years earlier. What Each Union Gets Out Of Signing Hedrick’s union is helping members claim compensation for hotel delays and get their expenses reimbursed. Having pilots back them publicly helps her bargaining position. She comes out looking tough, even though the note doesn’t go nearly as far as the union went in calling for leadership change earlier in the year. Silva gets a second union making his case that the people who fly the schedule know where it breaks. He opened contract talks a year early and asked for a seat on American’s board. When the pilots asked to make their case to the directors in February, the board sent them back to management. Weak profits are hurting employees. American paid 0.3% of eligible 2025 earnings in profit sharing. On $50,000 that’s $150. At Delta the same earnings would’ve meant $4,450. American already pays competitive pilot wages. I’d expect this negotiation to focus on quality of life issues rather than big raises. But the union is positioning itself to argue that management is at fault for poor performance, shouldn’t get to use that as an excuse for being unable to afford contract concessions, and the union is in fact part of the answer. United pilots got board representation in a 1994 employee buyout involving wage and work rule concessions. They kept it through bankruptcy as part of $1.1 billion in concessions. Delta pilots gained a voting seat in the Northwest merger deal. American’s pilots don’t have a transaction like that to bargain over. Meanwhile, the fight inside their independent union over joining the larger Air Line Pilots Association helped cost Silva’s predecessor his job. Silva wants to show effectiveness taking on management to keep his job.. Another pretty scathing letter put out by the Flight Attendants and Pilots Union at AA calling for new leadership — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 25, 2026 I wrote back in February that the unions would want credit for any change they saw coming. If American names a president in the coming weeks, Silva and Hedrick get to claim a victory and they’ve laid down a marker for what that leader needs to focus on. #6018. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6017. A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?

The serious issues underneath an unserious moral panic

Demonstrators hold signs depicting George Floyd during a protest against police brutality and racial inequality in Brooklyn, N.Y., June 13, 2020.

Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”

Playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes. “We know this listing has upset and offended many, and the fact that it made it onto our site has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet. For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement reads. In response to the post, some people have demanded that Playbill take more accountability by explaining exactly how such a thing was approved for the site, expose who is behind the musical (though that was already public), hire more minorities to prevent similar wrongdoing in the future, and issue apologies to the Floyd family and the black community. Others have more firmly called for barring the musical’s creative leader from the platform entirely.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

On “A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?”

Mendocino, a small coastal town in northern California, has welcomed its first points property. The nearly 50-year-old Hill House hotel was renovated and reopened in June 2026 as Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy — making it the first and only member of a major hotel loyalty program in Mendocino proper. (The closest options are members of IHG One Rewards and Wyndham Rewards in neighboring Fort Bragg.)

The Mendocino Coast region is known for its charming small-town vibes, natural beauty and outdoor pursuits, so the Trailborn brand’s laidback nature lodge concept fits in here like a seal in nearby Mendocino Bay. I stayed three nights in late October to get a first look at the property (and the town, which is on TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list).

Nestled just a few minutes’ walk outside downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino’s unassuming two-story buildings fit right in with the surrounding hotel scene. The design is inspired by nature — specifically, the redwood forests and tide pools of the surrounding Mendocino Coast — while still feeling modern and polished.

The grounds are bursting with native plants, many of them still in bloom when I visited in late October. Botanical art prints and zoological illustrations on the walls give a nod to the great outdoors, and curious guests can lose themselves in the lobby’s curiosity cabinet, a revamped relic of the original building. Visitors are encouraged to sign the guestbook with a stamp of a dried leaf or flower.

The hotel offers just 44 accommodations — relatively large for a Mendocino property — including 14 double queen rooms, 25 king rooms and 5 junior suites. Within each room type, travelers can choose to upgrade to features such as a balcony or deck, an ocean view or both.

My room, a spacious King Junior Suite Ocean View, felt like a relaxing retreat with its muted color palette of greens, browns and yellows and its cozy linen spa robes. After a day of exploring Mendocino, I enjoyed relaxing on the sofa, perusing the coffee table book Botanicum, and sampling locally made goodies from the snack basket and minibar (for a fee).

Trailborn Hill House has one on-site restaurant: Pizza Standard Time, a casual bar and diner offering mostly pizza, plus salads, charcuterie boards and small Italian bites like arancini. The fare was limited but tasty; my friend and I tried a pizza, salad, and local Husch chardonnay and were quite happy. It’s nice having a quick, casual meal available on-site in case you arrive late and tired from the drive, but it’s also just a few minutes’ walk to Mendocino if you want more options.

Like all Trailborn properties, this one offers a lobby convenience store called Hill House Wine & Grocer. Guests can purchase local drinks and snacks (mostly the kind you’d find on a charcuterie board), plus apparel, toys, candles with the property’s signature scent and other souvenirs.

The hotel also offered a small but delicious complimentary breakfast spread. As with everything else during my stay, the breakfast was high-quality yet unpretentious, with guests serving and bussing their own tables. Instead of having a designated breakfast area, guests can find a cozy spot to eat inside Pizza Standard Time or the attached Cabot Cove Detective Library, outside by one of the fire pits or back to their room.

However, this will change when Trailborn’s second Mendocino property, The Mendocino Hotel, opens in 2027. Instead of complimentary breakfast, Hill House plans to provide guests with a voucher to Moonwave, The Mendocino Hotel’s dining concept, which will serve “coastal comfort” food three meals a day plus drinks at the lobby bar.

If you didn’t realize you were in a small town, you will as soon as you interact with any of the hotel staff — everyone I spoke to, from front desk staff to custodians, was beyond friendly.

As for amenities, they align with the brand’s laid-back, outdoorsy style and with some of the things the Mendocino area is known for. You’ll find:

Located just a few minutes’ walk (or bike ride) from downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn puts guests in the heart of the town’s charming boutiques and varied dining and drinking scene. But you won’t get bored if you hang around the property, either.

Here are some of the on-site activities guests may want to try:

While Mendocino’s remoteness makes it a haven for crowd-weary travelers, it’s becoming easier than ever to reach thanks to recent roadwork funding and new direct flights to Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), including on Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest. That’s one reason Mendo made TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list.

But travelers can also fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC), which are a bit farther away but offer more flight options.

Depending on the airport you choose, you’ll need to rent a car and drive two to four hours to Mendocino.

Basic rooms start as low as $140 per night in the off-season, while my King Junior Suite Ocean View starts around $350 per night (though these prices can climb much higher on summer weekends). Award rates start at 48,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night, or you could redeem a 50,000-point free night certificate.

When booking, you’ll want to use one of the credit cards that earn the most points for Marriott stays, as well as one that possibly offers automatic Marriott Bonvoy elite status for value-added benefits. These include:

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hill House has three wheelchair-accessible rooms, including two double queens and one king; these feature accessible tubs and, in some cases, roll-in showers. The property and its parking lot are also wheelchair accessible. For hearing-impaired guests, a portable kit can be installed in any room.

As a points traveler who loves Mendocino, I’m thrilled to see the town’s first points property not only opening but thriving. As a traveler who appreciates unique stays and has experienced some of the town’s charming independent properties, I’m also glad that Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino has brought enough character to fit seamlessly into the local scene.

It seems the Trailborn brand — and Marriott Bonvoy — is betting big on Mendocino. Hill House is one of two Mendocino properties purchased by The Trailborn brand. The second, the 150-year-old Mendocino Hotel, is undergoing renovation and slated to open in 2027.

#6015. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

IndiGo is adding more flights to Southeast Asia at a time when rising fuel costs and geopolitical tensions are making some of its westbound operations more expensive.

Southeast Asia suits the airline's narrowbody fleet and short flying times, while Pakistan's airspace closure since April 2025 has made westbound routes from Delhi longer and more expensive. IndiGo still targets international flying at roughly 40% of capacity by 2030, up from about one-third today.

Developers in the UAE are still launching branded residences, betting on long-term demand as the U.S.-Iran war that began in late February weighs on Dubai’s hotel market.

Branded residences are residential properties developed in partnership with an established brand, such as a luxury hotel operator.

#6009. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#6007. Culture Is Driving New Interest in Travel for Ramadan

Longer stays and a rise in cultural visits suggest Ramadan is becoming a more significant season in Abu Dhabi’s tourism calendar. The Department of Culture and Tourism - DCT Abu Dhabi now sees an opportunity to turn the holy month into a more deliberate travel proposition for both visitors and the global travel trade.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Ramadan has traditionally been viewed as a quieter month for travel in the Gulf. However, early data from DCT Abu Dhabi’s Ramadan 2026 season suggests that old assumptions about the holy month may be changing. The average length of stay across Abu Dhabi increased 3% year-on-year, while domestic hotel guests stayed 31% longer. Visits to cultural institutions more than doubled, rising from around 131,000 in Ramadan 2025 to over 291,000 in 2026.

Skift Studio spoke with Abdulla Yousuf, director of international operations at DCT Abu Dhabi, to explore how the emirate is making Ramadan a more intentional part of the visitor experience.

Skift Studio: How have international visitors and the travel trade traditionally viewed visiting Abu Dhabi during Ramadan, and how has that changed in recent years?

Abdulla Yousuf: Some international travelers and travel trade partners have historically viewed Ramadan as a period when activity may be lower across the region, especially regarding opening hours, dining options, and the availability of visitor experiences. We’ve collectively worked on changing that perception over the past few years. Abu Dhabi remains open during Ramadan. Our world-class hotels, cultural landmarks, theme parks, dining venues, and beaches remain open without interruption throughout the Holy Month.

What changes during Ramadan is not operational capacity, but the emirate’s rhythm. It transforms into a culturally rich season of community and reflection during the day, which gives way to an electric, festive atmosphere after sunset. The travel trade is increasingly recognizing that Ramadan is a value-added cultural window that cannot be experienced at any other time of the year.

Abu Dhabi saw an increase in the average length of stay during Ramadan 2026. What do you take from that change, and what factors do you think may have influenced it?

One likely contributing factor was the timing of Ramadan within Abu Dhabi’s cooler season, when comfortable temperatures make it easier to enjoy outdoor activities, such as waterfront promenades, kayaking in the mangroves, desert adventures, and visits to heritage sites.

At the same time, Ramadan reshapes the emirate into a distinctive day-to-night journey. Calm daytime exploration of beaches, resorts, and world-class attractions transitions into evenings centered around iftars, atmospheric night markets, community suhoors, and cultural activations like Layali Nights.

Extended opening hours make every day feel varied, immersive, and rewarding, naturally encouraging visitors to stay longer. This variety gives travel advisors and tour operators more opportunities to build itineraries that combine relaxation, culture, and outdoor experiences, helping position Abu Dhabi as a destination worth visiting during Ramadan.

What does the 2026 data tell you about how different visitor segments are using the destination?

The figures highlight two interesting trends. Visitors are spending longer in Abu Dhabi, and engagement with our cultural offering has increased significantly. The 31% year-on-year increase in length of stay among domestic hotel guests underscores the potential for Ramadan to drive longer stays in the domestic market. The increase in visits to our cultural institutions reinforces the importance of culture within the destination’s Ramadan offering.

The opportunity for our international travel trade partners is in communicating this diversity more effectively. Ramadan can appeal to visitors interested in culture, family experiences, hospitality, and outdoor activities, allowing partners to tailor itineraries to different traveler interests rather than treating the Holy Month as a single type of travel experience.

What role does culture play in Abu Dhabi’s Ramadan visitor experience?

Culture is central to the Ramadan experience in Abu Dhabi. The Holy Month offers visitors an opportunity not only to discover our cultural attractions but also to experience Emirati traditions, hospitality, and the importance of community firsthand.

Culture during the Holy Month is lived and shared. During the day, visitors explore landmarks such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, Zayed National Museum and Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in Saadiyat Cultural District.

It becomes deeply communal at night, from heritage games at Al Jahili Fort and Ramadan at Qasr Al Hosn to shared iftars at Ezba Experiences, and late-night visits to Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque.

What makes Ramadan a great time to visit Abu Dhabi? What should visitors expect?

Visitors can expect a deeply authentic experience. First and foremost, Abu Dhabi is completely open for business. Every luxury resort, Michelin-recognized restaurant, shopping destination, and major attraction functions at full capacity with world-class hospitality.

After sunset, the emirate becomes remarkably vibrant. Dining evolves into a shared celebration, with iftars showcasing both global and Emirati flavors, followed by suhoors that invite people to slow down, connect, and enjoy live music, conversation, and warm hospitality late into the night. Above all, Emirati culture is rooted in generosity. International visitors are invited to sit at communal tables and build genuine connections with our community.

With Ramadan 2027 also falling during Abu Dhabi’s cooler season (February to March), visitors can combine these cultural experiences with time outdoors, whether exploring the Corniche, enjoying our beaches or discovering the desert.

My advice to anyone considering a visit is to embrace the distinct rhythm of the Holy Month. Ramadan offers a chance to discover Abu Dhabi at a slightly slower pace, while experiencing traditions and moments of community that make this time of year special.

What are you hearing from tour operators and travel advisors about selling Abu Dhabi during Ramadan? Where do knowledge gaps still exist, and how does the Experience Abu Dhabi Experts Ramadan module respond to them?

Some of the questions we encounter relate to practical considerations, such as opening hours, dining options, and the experiences available to visitors during the Holy Month. To address this, our International Operations team provides practical information and opportunities for first-hand experience of the destination. Our Experience Abu Dhabi Experts e-learning platform includes dedicated Ramadan training to help advisors better understand the visitor experience and communicate it to their clients.

We complement this with international trade engagement, including workshops in 23 markets, roadshows, and familiarisation trips that allow our partners to experience Abu Dhabi and its cultural offerings for themselves.

Ultimately, our role is to help the travel trade move beyond general awareness of Abu Dhabi and develop a deeper understanding of the destination. The better equipped our partners are to explain what visitors can experience during Ramadan, the more confidently they can recommend it and develop relevant itineraries.

How will DCT Abu Dhabi use learnings from Ramadan 2026 to shape the destination’s approach in 2027 and beyond?

The results from Ramadan 2026 have reinforced the importance of positioning the Holy Month as a distinctive part of Abu Dhabi’s year-round visitor offering. The increases in average length of stay and cultural engagement are encouraging and provide insights as we continue developing our approach for 2027 and beyond.

One priority is to continue working with our tourism and hospitality partners to showcase the range of experiences available during Ramadan, from cultural attractions and outdoor activities to evening dining and community celebrations.

Our wider ambition remains aligned with Abu Dhabi’s Tourism Strategy 2030: to attract visitors year-round, encourage longer stays, and strengthen the emirate’s position as a leading global destination. Ramadan plays an important role in that ambition by offering international visitors a culturally distinctive, uniquely Abu Dhabi experience.

#6006. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

#6005. How Amadeus Pulled Away From Sabre and Travelport

Photo Credit: Amadeus has outpaced its rivals.  Grok

Amadeus gained distribution share and built a bigger airline IT business. Sabre and Travelport remain weighed down by heavy debt and a heavier reliance on distribution.

For decades, the companies that controlled airline distribution occupied one of the most important positions in the travel industry. But making money from travel bookings and building a profitable technology business around them have turned out to be very different propositions. The contrasting fortunes of Amadeus, Sabre, and Travelport show just how different.

In 2000, Amadeus accounted for an estimated 26% of global GDS air bookings, compared with 34% for Sabre, including Abacus. Galileo and Worldspan, then separate systems that were later combined into Travelport, together had about 40%. By 2023, the estimates were 47% for Amadeus, 32% for Sabre, and 21% for Travelport, according to Redburn Atlantic data.

Three companies that once split global airline distribution between them now look nothing alike. Amadeus has moved from an estimated 26% of GDS air bookings in 2000 to 47% in 2023, according to Redburn Atlantic data, while Sabre slipped from 34% to 32% and the Galileo-Worldspan combination that became Travelport fell from about 40% to 21%. The bigger divergence is in what each company sells. Amadeus generated €6.52 billion ($7.15 billion) in 2025, with only €3.12 billion from air distribution and the rest from airline IT and hospitality technology built through Altéa, Navitaire, Newmarket International, and TravelClick. Sabre generated $2.77 billion from continuing operations, 80% of it distribution, and sold Hospitality Solutions to TPG for $1.1 billion in 2025 to pay down debt. Travelport reported $1.44 billion, nearly 90% of it booking fees. All of this played out in a channel that shrank: Amadeus processed 580.4 million travel-agency air bookings in 2019 and 484.5 million in 2025, a decline of about 17%, even as airline passenger traffic recovered. In mid-November 2026, Amadeus carried a stock-market value of roughly $29 billion against less than $1 billion for Sabre.

#6004. Huang’s Surprise Return Doesn’t End Nvidia Questions

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026.

Well, that was quick. Less than two weeks after unanimously accepting CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board has now, again unanimously, agreed to reinstate him. This followed “a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” The first hurdle must have been trickier than the second. Presumably even more importantly, based on “input” from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, the board was “confident” that Huang’s return posed “no national security risk.”

President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation. In a post on Truth Social, he argued that it was needed “in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy.”

On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars. The tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 6.5 percent, the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent. Trump views the stock market as a critical indicator of the nation’s economic health, not without reason, including the “wealth effect” created by rising stock prices. Booms can go bust, but, although calculating the effect of the AI build-out on the economy is not straightforward, by some estimates it may account for a quarter or more of current GDP growth.

Trump also wrote that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Huang’s “return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump added that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of [its] compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect U.S. national security.” And so it should.

Various government agencies are investigating, as are a number of congressional committees. It was also announced on Monday that the U.S. is prohibiting the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm previously connected to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Nvidia’s CEO was in a relationship. The concern is that Megaspeed may have been diverting contraband chips to China. More generally, the administration has already tightened the rules governing exports of such chips to other countries where there is a diversion risk, a welcome, if overdue, step, as is the closing of the loophole that allowed enterprises in China and other hostile states to have remote access to the power of advanced American AI chips from businesses located in third countries.

This is a saga with a lot to unpack, much of which remains, at best, guesswork. Nevertheless, we do know (or can be pretty sure that) Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang considerable leeway when it came to the way he ran Nvidia, not least with regard to the way that so much of the company’s decision-making was concentrated in him. That may well have underpinned Nvidia’s extraordinary success — a win for the U.S., as well as for Nvidia — but it also clearly played an important part in the current imbroglio and raises troubling questions about the consequences were Huang to step down again or, even if he weathers this crisis, at some later stage. It is said that no man is irreplaceable, but that is not always so.

We also know that Nvidia, sometimes referred to as AI’s central bank, has played a key role in supporting the growth of earlier-stage companies. This has been criticized as a form of circular financing by Nvidia (the company is helping fund some of its client base), but it has played a vital part in the creation of an American AI ecosystem. Through Nvidia, Huang was a critical element in this ecosystem’s growth.

And we know that the success of the American AI sector has geopolitical as well as commercial implications. There is an AI race between China and the U.S. The U.S. must hang on to the lead it has built up — here’s the catch — in no small part with Nvidia’s assistance. Huang has argued against overly broad U.S. restrictions on the export of U.S. chips, arguing that they will only encourage China to make their own, an unconvincing argument given the importance Beijing puts on autarky. Of course, Nvidia would benefit financially (for a while) by selling AI chips to China, but it is not in our strategic interest to allow it.

Huang is entitled to his views, but they do not entitle his company to evade U.S, export controls or even to turn a blind eye should Nvidia’s customers “divert” chips to forbidden destinations. The question of whether this occurred will almost certainly be the main focus of the investigations. It is a question that dwarfs (however much corporate governance purists may object) Huang’s reckless choice of companionship and, in this respect, his lack of candor with Nvidia’s board. The investigations will lead where they will lead. They will also be highly politicized. Regardless of the investigations’ conclusions, they will be a major distraction and, as such, unhelpful to Nvidia and the U.S. AI sector more broadly. That will be a win that should never have been handed to Beijing.

#5998. Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images)

That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

“It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

“I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

“You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”

Trump, who was convicted by a New York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

“In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

“This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”

Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”

“The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”

Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

“I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

“I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

“Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”

On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

“You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”

John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

#5996. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Your Questions Answered

Questions from attendees. Answers by Skift Intelligence.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S. airline revenue architecture, and it’s now at the crowded end of its growth curve. Premium cabins generated $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue, in 2024, and U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy. The open question is no longer demand. It’s whether every carrier scaling premium at once dilutes the yields that made it work. 12

The behavior behind it is capital, not talk. United ordered more than 250 aircraft with more business class and premium economy, Delta is spending $1 billion on new Delta One suites arriving in early 2027, American is flying retrofitted 777-300ERs, Alaska is adding business class on widebodies and select narrowbodies plus its first premium economy, and JetBlue is launching domestic first class 345.

The results follow the spend. Delta’s premium cabins hit 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024, with premium revenue up about 57% over that stretch to $6.9 billion 6. Delta held a 9.5% operating margin through the fuel shock on fares, premium mix, loyalty, and non-flying revenue 7.

Premium is also being unbundled, which is the clearest sign it has become normal pricing infrastructure rather than a flagship product. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, extending segmentation it already applied to Polaris and Premium Plus 8. United CFO Michael Leskinen said “all of society is becoming more premium,” citing hotels, cruise lines, and car service 9.

The front cabin keeps growing but stops being one product. Tiered business fares let carriers sell the seat to price-sensitive buyers without discounting the full experience, which protects yield as capacity rises.

Skift Research’s main caution is oversupply rather than demand weakness. If carriers scale premium simultaneously, especially long-haul, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to trade up and dilute the premium.

With jet fuel averaging $4.50 a gallon and domestic fares up about 32% year over year, carriers without premium and loyalty levers are the exposed ones. Deutsche Bank expects American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier to lose money in 2026.

Premium demand in the U.S. is structural, built on a K-shaped income recovery and self-funded leisure travelers rather than corporate accounts alone. What’s cyclical is the return on it, and that depends on how much premium seating the industry adds from here.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The U.S. market supports two fully funded premium airlines today — Delta and United — and a contested third seat that American, Alaska, and JetBlue are all spending into at the worst possible moment. Premium demand is real and large, but Skift Research warns the risk ahead is oversupply, not weak demand. Fuel at record levels is deciding who can keep paying for the buildout. 921

Premium cabins generate $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue, and Delta drew 50% of passenger revenue from premium in the second quarter 3. United has grown premium seat capacity 46% since 2019, closing on Delta’s lead 5. The economics behind the third seat are much weaker: Deutsche Bank expects Delta, United, Southwest, and Allegiant to be profitable in 2026, while American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier lose money — American and JetBlue by roughly $1 billion pretax each 2.

Sources: Q3 margins and revenue growth 6; American’s results 1; Alaska’s losses and premium plan 78; JetBlue’s first class 2.

Two carriers are monetizing premium; three more are buying the seats and hoping the returns arrive. Skift Research classifies premium as a peaking trend whose main forward risk is yield dilution if everyone scales at once — which is close to what is happening now.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Loyalty cash isn’t going away — Delta took $8.2 billion from Amex in 2025 and Air Canada just had Aeroplan valued at C$10 billion, more than the airline itself. But the economics are less proven than the headline numbers suggest, the regulatory and AI risks are real, and premium cabins are now the faster-growing engine at $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue. 135

Two things are true at once. The cash from banks is enormous and disclosed; the net profit behind it is not. United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the “credit card company that happens to fly planes” framing, arguing analysts count what banks pay for miles but ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers — “Nobody counts the cost,” he said 1. Skift’s review of filings found American collected $6.2 billion from card and other partners, while United doesn’t publish total bank cash at all, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 7.2% of passenger miles in 2019 to 10.3% in 2025 1.

The clearest structural alternative is premium. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as a peaking trend airlines should scale now, with over 70% of travelers saying they would trade up and Delta’s premium revenue up nearly 50% since 2019 10. American’s Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 6.

The loyalty engine is being stress-tested from three directions at once: disclosure (nobody shows the net), regulation (uncapped U.S. interchange fees that the Credit Card Competition Act would put at risk), and discovery (AI making fares and benefits easier to compare). None of those kill it. All three argue against treating card remuneration as the only growth story.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American has closed a lot of product gaps on paper and almost none of the financial ones. Its premium seat mix is already high — roughly 30% of seats generating about 50% of revenue 4 — but Delta converts premium and loyalty into profit at a scale American doesn’t approach 1.

CEO Robert Isom now calls American a “premium global airline,” a label adopted in press releases in December 2025.

Premium drove roughly two-thirds of Delta’s passenger-revenue growth, and Delta expects premium revenue to pass main cabin by 2027.

American’s chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate returns that fund the next round of investment and pay down debt, and that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 2 3. That is the condition American hasn’t met yet.

American is closing the product gap on a timeline that runs into the early 2030s while Delta compounds the loyalty and margin advantage now. The risk is crowding: with United, Alaska, and most major international carriers expanding premium cabins at once, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to pay up, and yields come under pressure.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

The premium shift is real and durable, but it is late in its growth, not early. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as “peaking” — a trend to scale now, with oversupply rather than demand weakness as the main risk. It runs as long as capacity discipline holds and the wealth effect behind it holds. The thing that ends it is airlines all expanding the front of the plane at once, diluting yields. 12

The evidence for durability is in the revenue, not the rhetoric. Premium cabins generated $188 billion in 2024, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 1. Delta’s premium cabins reached 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024 3. Air Canada’s premium share has gone from about 20% a decade ago to roughly 30%, with a 35% target by 2030 4. The addressable market widened beyond corporate accounts: Skift Research found more than 70% of travelers say they would trade up, with self-funded leisure travelers driving the growth 1.

The supply response is where the clock starts. U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy 1. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft 5. Virgin Atlantic is taking refurbished 787s from 192 economy seats to 127 and removing its onboard bars for more premium seats 67. Turkish Airlines is adding premium economy in 2028, leaving Qatar and Etihad among the few long-haul holdouts 3. Alaska is adding premium economy for the first time even after fuel wiped out first-half profit 8.

Unbundling the front cabin keeps yields up without adding seats. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, following Delta, JetBlue, Etihad, Air France, KLM, and Qatar. Air Canada has unbundled business and premium economy and sells legroom in economy.

ZS’s Kunal Shah said the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

Premium is now a baseline revenue assumption rather than a stopgap, so the question is no longer whether it lasts but who gets squeezed when everyone’s retrofits land at once. The carriers that survive the dilution will be the ones segmenting inside every cabin instead of just adding seats at the front.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

No contradiction. American removed international first class from its 777-300ERs to fit 70 Flagship Suites per aircraft — trading a handful of ultra-premium seats for far more business class inventory. The math favors density at the top of the cabin: premium seats are about 30% of American’s fleet and generate roughly 50% of revenue, and premium revenue grew 22.9% in Q3 versus 19.5% in main cabin. 758

American announced the first class removal back in 2022, framing it then as paying for a 30% increase in premium seats on the 777s and a 63% increase on the 787-9s 8. The retrofitted 777-300ERs now flying carry 70 business class seats 4. International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air New Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

The real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4.
